text:
Happy belated Veterans Day — and a deep, heartfelt 🙏 Thank you!!!!!
I just watched this short but extraordinary interview with Lieutenant Brad Snyder on NBC10 Philadelphia’s Philly Live, and it stayed with me. What a beautiful man. What a beautiful human being. The kind of person who makes you stop, feel a little smaller in the best way, and feel genuinely honored that people like him walk this earth while we are here to share it with them.
Snyder is a Navy veteran, Naval Academy graduate, former Explosive Ordnance Disposal officer who served in Iraq and Afghanistan, and an eight-time Paralympic medalist (six gold, two silver). On September 7, 2011, while embedded with special operations forces in Afghanistan and helping wounded partners, he was blinded by a massive IED. Exactly one year later, to the day, he stood on the London Paralympic podium as a gold medalist. He later added more swimming medals in Rio, transitioned to paratriathlon, and won gold again in Tokyo. He has written a book about the journey, speaks on leadership and adversity, and continues to serve in new ways — including, on this night, as honorary captain for the 76ers’ military appreciation night.
In the interview he doesn’t dwell on the injury or the medals. He talks about how the military taught him to treat every new challenge — bomb school, jump training, sudden blindness, learning to swim or do triathlon without sight — as simply the next thing to master. He talks about the harder work of rebuilding confidence once the uniform comes off, realizing that what remains is character, the ability to lead people toward shared purpose, and the capacity to keep giving. Sports, he says, gave him validation that he still had something left to offer his community and his country. And that is what drives him now: sharing the story so others can tackle hard things and navigate adversity with grace.
What moved me most was his simple, clear view of Veterans Day. He is proud of the special night with the Sixers and Team Toyota, but he points out that every single moment, tens of thousands of service members are deployed somewhere in the world — away from their families, sleep-deprived, not eating well — preserving the ordinary freedoms and security the rest of us get to take for granted. Taking even a moment to be grateful for them, he says, is magical. His advice to anyone struggling to find purpose is equally quiet and powerful: make the most of every interaction. We all have the ability to empower, love, and inspire one another in the ordinary moments of a day.
He loves the Sixers. He’s here, in the area, with his family nearby, serving as honorary captain for their military appreciation night. There is something especially warm and local about that — a man of his caliber choosing to show up, smile, say “Go Sixers,” and use the platform to shine a light on those still serving. It feels personal. It feels like ours.
I cherish people like Lieutenant Brad Snyder. In a world that can feel noisy, cynical, and quick to depreciate sacrifice, he is living proof of steadiness, humility, and continued service. He took one of the hardest possible turns life can hand someone and kept moving forward with purpose, without self-pity, and with a genuine desire to lift others. Watching him speak — calm, grateful, focused on the people still out there and on the simple act of bringing out the best in one another — is a reminder of the best of what we are capable of.
To Lieutenant Snyder: thank you for your service, for your example, and for the way you carry yourself. To every veteran, every active-duty service member, and every military family: thank you. The life so many of us get to live is possible because of people like you. We are honored to share the earth with you while we are here.
Go Sixers. And thank you.

text:
Recenty interview of $RKLB CEO @Peter_J_Beck with @FunOfInvesting 

Q1. Was there anything in Rocket Lab's latest earnings report or earnings call that you felt didn't receive enough attention from retail investors or institutional investors?

Peter Beck:

I think people pretty much understood the results. Selling $1 billion worth of launches in a quarter is a significant achievement.

One slide we're particularly proud of shows our continued execution and growth year after year. It's one thing to have a strong growth year followed by a flat year and then another strong year. What's impressive is seeing consistent growth year after year.

We're approaching nearly $1 billion in revenue this year, and I think the entire team is very proud of that achievement.

Q2. Neutron was originally targeted for 2024 and is now expected in 2027. What have you learned throughout the development process, and what gives you confidence in the revised timeline?

Peter Beck:

I've learned that I'm not particularly good at estimating timelines for medium-class launch vehicles.

In all seriousness, Rocket Lab operates with an optimistic approach to scheduling. We use what's called a green-light schedule, which assumes everything goes well, with no development issues along the way. That represents the earliest possible delivery timeline.

The philosophy is that if you build too much buffer into a schedule, you inevitably consume it. By not building in excessive buffer, you give yourself the best opportunity to deliver on time.

We've encountered challenges along the way, particularly because we're developing technologies that nobody has done before. Rocket development is difficult, and delays are part of the process. However, I think our timeline is relatively normal compared with the history of rocket development.

I'd much rather discover an issue with a rocket tank during ground testing than discover it during flight.

Our development philosophy is also different. We're not simply trying to get the first rocket onto the launch pad. We want the second, third, fourth, and fifth rockets to follow quickly. We've been investing in the processes and infrastructure needed to make that possible.

Q3. What is Rocket Lab doing today to prepare for scaling Neutron beyond its first flight? What are the biggest challenges in transitioning from the first launch to a regular launch business?

Peter Beck:

One way to evaluate the seriousness of a rocket program is to look at its investment in recovery barges.

A barge is far more complicated than a floating piece of steel. It requires megawatts of power generation, thrusters, autonomous capabilities, and the ability to maintain its position within sub-meter accuracy in the Atlantic Ocean.

Building a barge is a two-to-three-year investment, so getting started early is extremely important.

We've also invested heavily in factories and manufacturing infrastructure. For example, our engine factory can now produce an engine in a matter of days.

Another important part of our strategy is how we approach manufacturing. Traditionally, we would build one component, test it, confirm that it works, and then build the second one.

However, that serial approach takes time.

For components we're highly confident won't change, we've already built multiple units. For components with more uncertainty, we're still building more than one, but we're taking a measured approach because some of those components could ultimately be scrapped.

This is the fastest way to scale production and prepare for a regular launch cadence.

Q4. How many annual Neutron launches would Rocket Lab need to become profitable?

Peter Beck:

The economics turn positive relatively quickly, particularly at a launch price of $70 million.

We expect to cover the costs of the overall operation at a relatively low launch cadence, well below 10 launches per year.

Our target gross margin model for Neutron is similar to Electron: approximately 50%.

Two factors primarily influence launch profitability:

Launch cadence: Higher launch frequency allows us to spread fixed costs across more launches, including facilities and launch infrastructure. This is particularly important for Electron because it isn't reusable.

Reusability: Neutron benefits from reusability, which allows us to amortize infrastructure and operational costs more quickly.

As launch cadence increases, the economics become increasingly attractive.

Q5. Neutron's $70 million launch price surprised some investors. Is this driven by supply-demand dynamics, or is there an upper limit to what customers are willing to pay?

Peter Beck:

It's a combination of factors.

Launch capacity is scarce, and we have a limited number of available slots. That makes those slots extremely valuable.

From the beginning of the Neutron program, I said we would sell our first launches when we could command full price.

Naturally, customers expect discounts for rockets that haven't flown yet, particularly during the early stages of development when there's no physical hardware available to inspect.

However, everything has worked out as we expected. We wanted to enter a market where demand for launch services was already very strong, and we had no intention of discounting Neutron.

Not a single Neutron launch has been discounted. In fact, we've seen the opposite.

When customers evaluate launch vehicles currently in development, only two companies have successfully demonstrated the ability to take a rocket from a clean-sheet design to a high-cadence launch vehicle. Rocket Lab is one of them.

When customers visit us, see our hardware, and understand our track record, they have confidence that we can deliver.

Q6. Rocket Lab's acquisition of Iridium is expected to close in mid-2027. What are the biggest integration challenges, and how long will it take for operational synergies to translate into financial results?

Peter Beck:

Some synergies will translate immediately. For example, there are straightforward opportunities to eliminate duplicated corporate functions between two public companies.

The bigger challenge is that Iridium is a relatively large acquisition. Its employee headcount is approximately twice that of the largest company we've previously acquired and integrated, which was SolAero.

However, SolAero and Iridium share similarities. Both are traditional space companies with long operating histories.

I think we did an excellent job integrating SolAero, and I expect the same with Iridium.

The more interesting challenge is that Rocket Lab is primarily made up of rocket and satellite engineers, whereas Iridium is a services company.

One of the reasons we decided to acquire rather than build this capability ourselves is Iridium's tremendous customer base and expertise in operating space-based services businesses.

We'll work alongside their team and learn from their experience.

Longer term, the opportunity is significant. When you own your own rocket, build your own satellites, and operate services from space, you create a powerful business model.

Combining the two companies will allow us to bring new services and programs to market that Iridium could not have pursued independently.

Q7. Looking three to five years ahead, how meaningful could the operational synergies become?

Peter Beck:

I certainly hope it doesn't take three to five years. That's an extraordinarily long timeframe for Rocket Lab. I measure this in months, not years.

Both teams have already identified numerous exciting services and opportunities that we can pursue as a combined company.

I also want to emphasize that our ambition isn't simply to become the world's leading safety-critical communications company.

Communications will be one important part of our services business, but you should expect Rocket Lab to offer multiple services in the future.

Q8. Rocket Lab has discussed potentially dedicating half of Neutron's launch capacity to its own satellite services. How do you balance near-term revenue from external launches against the opportunity to generate larger recurring revenue streams from operating your own satellites?

Peter Beck:

We approach this very carefully because there is still a significant shortage of launch capacity in the industry.

We need to continue providing launch services to the broader space community. Given the size of our Space Systems business, limited launch availability would also negatively affect national security and commercial programs.

We will always ensure that a steady supply of launch capacity remains available to the industry.

At the same time, we need to preserve enough capacity to pursue our own opportunities.

There is an important economic distinction here. Launching someone else's satellite generates a one-time revenue opportunity. Launching our own satellite can create recurring revenue for the next 10 years.

The economics of launching your own infrastructure are significantly stronger over the long term.

However, we must balance that opportunity against our responsibility to support the broader space industry, which also affects other parts of our business.

Q9. Rocket Lab has signed StarCloud as a Neutron customer, but you've expressed skepticism about the economics of large-scale orbital data centers. Is this a market Rocket Lab intends to pursue as a meaningful future revenue opportunity?

Peter Beck:

Sometimes it's great to be a pioneer, and sometimes it's better to stay slightly behind the front line and observe how things develop.

I've been proven wrong on multiple occasions, so I wouldn't take my comments about this market as gospel.

I'm an engineer first and probably an entrepreneur second. Naturally, I approach new technologies with a healthy degree of skepticism.

We're certainly participating in the market, and if orbital data centers turn out to be a significant opportunity, I think Rocket Lab is in an excellent position to execute.

However, for now, I'd rather be a fast follower than lead the market.

Q10. So, if orbital data centers become a major market, Rocket Lab will participate, but it's not an immediate strategic priority?

Peter Beck:

I'm certainly not going to bet the business on it.

We're happy to support other companies, as we've already demonstrated. We're watching the market closely and will contribute where appropriate.

If it becomes a genuinely significant opportunity, we'll pursue it.

Q11. As government satellite programs approach completion, how much future growth do you expect from repeat orders and constellation replacements versus winning entirely new contracts?

Peter Beck:

One attractive aspect of defense contracts is that many of these programs have bipartisan support. They involve capabilities that the country desperately needs.

As a result, they're relatively resilient to changes in political administrations.

These platforms have defined operational lifetimes and eventually need to be replaced.

Additionally, as threats evolve, countermeasures and defense capabilities must evolve as well.

The defense industry is never static. As adversaries develop new technologies, new capabilities and countermeasures become necessary.

Unlike some commercial satellite applications, where infrastructure can remain unchanged for a long time, defense systems require continuous development and modernization.

I therefore expect a relatively consistent stream of opportunities and contracts in this market.

Q12. Following the midterm elections, do you anticipate increased congressional scrutiny or efforts to diversify government contractors, potentially creating new opportunities for Rocket Lab?

Peter Beck:

I think the environment will remain relatively agnostic.

There is strong bipartisan support for many space-based defense missions, and I don't believe anyone will eliminate programs that are critically important to national security.

Historically, these programs have remained relatively consistent despite changes in government.

Q13. Do you expect defense and national security to become a larger part of the global space industry?

Peter Beck:

Yes, but perhaps in a different way.

Unfortunately, we're living in increasingly fragile geopolitical times.

One of the most common things we hear from our friends and allies outside the United States is that they want sovereign space capabilities.

This is particularly true in Europe.

That's one of the reasons we established Rocket Lab Europe and made the Mynaric acquisition. We're working to establish a strong foothold in Europe because we see it as a major future market, particularly for defense and national security applications.

Q14. What is the biggest misconception investors have about Rocket Lab today?

Peter Beck:

I think the misconception is actually in the company's name.

Everyone assumes Rocket Lab is primarily about rockets. In some respects, that's understandable because without rockets, you can't do much in space.

Launch is an extremely difficult business, but having access to space gives you the ability to do so much more.

A significant portion of our business has nothing to do with rockets. We have a substantial Space Systems business, and soon we'll have an even larger presence in space services.

Perhaps I should have called the company Space Lab instead of Rocket Lab!

Q15. How large do you see the services business becoming, particularly following the Iridium acquisition?

Peter Beck:

Services will eventually dwarf everything else by a significant margin.

If you look at the total addressable markets:

Launch: Approximately $10 billion.
Space Systems: Approximately $30 billion.
Space Services: Approximately $320 billion.

Depending on which industry estimates you look at, the space services market could exceed $1 trillion by 2035.

Space services have always represented the largest opportunity. After all, providing services is ultimately the reason we go to space.

Q16. Rocket Lab has developed a very passionate retail investor following. Is there anything you believe the market misunderstands about the company, or any message you'd like to share with retail shareholders?

Peter Beck:

First, I'd like to thank everyone for their support and belief in the company. We genuinely appreciate it and take that responsibility very seriously.

There's nothing more rewarding than hearing stories from shareholders who invested at $3.80, maintained their conviction in the company, and have done well enough to achieve meaningful milestones, such as buying a house.

Those stories are fantastic.

We take our responsibility to shareholders extremely seriously.

At the end of the day, our job is to create shareholder value.

Space is exciting, and what we're building is incredible, but the company must ultimately become profitable, financially robust, and sustainable over the long term.

That is our number one priority: creating value for shareholders.

text:
Vlad, I think you’ve fundamentally mischaracterized AST SpaceMobile’s strategic position. You’ve taken one legitimate industry constraint and constructed an entirely backward narrative around it.

$ASTS isn’t being forced into building rockets because it has nowhere else to turn. It has already secured launch agreements covering more than 100 BlueBird satellites through 2028, involving SpaceX, Blue Origin and others. Blue Origin publicly advertises its multiyear relationship with AST SpaceMobile. Those relationships aren’t disappearing when Blacklift arrives.

Blacklift is additive, not a rescue operation.

Consider the actual strategic trajectory. AST has developed proprietary satellite technology, demonstrated direct-to-device broadband capabilities, established relationships with major mobile network operators, expanded into sovereign and government markets, and is now vertically integrating launch.

That isn’t a company running out of options. It’s a company accumulating them.

And the implications extend far beyond launch availability.

Blacklift offers control over deployment cadence, mission-specific vehicle optimization, launch flexibility, and potentially dramatically lower marginal costs as flight rates scale. AST has even acquired perpetual manufacturing rights to the engines. This is industrial integration across an increasingly differentiated technology platform.

Meanwhile, AST’s addressable market is expanding beyond conventional cellular broadband into sovereign infrastructure, defense, AI-enabled services, radar, sensing and other space-based capabilities. The implications for orbital infrastructure demand are enormous.

You correctly identify launch scarcity as an industry constraint. But you’ve overlooked the much bigger opportunity: AST can continue purchasing launch services while developing the ability to internalize their economics.

And importantly, this is not some clean-sheet engine development fantasy. AST is leveraging existing Miranda and Vira engine architecture and Firefly’s engineering capabilities. The 2028 target is ambitious, certainly, but ambition and desperation are not synonyms.

The possibility of a multi-trillion-dollar enterprise remains speculative. But if AST ultimately achieves that scale, this kind of vertical integration could become one of the defining strategic decisions that made it possible.

You’re looking at Blacklift as evidence of AST’s disadvantage.

I’d suggest you’re witnessing the opposite: a company with an unusually differentiated technology platform building the industrial infrastructure to capture an opportunity far larger than its original business model.

This isn’t AST playing the only hand it holds. It’s AST expanding the number of hands it can play, while retaining the ones it already has.

An AI-native company should be designed around 5 principles:

1. Own the context: 
Biz data, relationships, rules, and history are accessible through a coherent system.

2. Automate the operations: 
Agents and deterministic workflows perform as much routine work as reliably possible.

3. Buy the primitives: 
Use established infra and specialized services where building offers little advantage.

4. Generate the experiences: 
Create human interfaces when and where they deliver value.

5. Govern the autonomy: 
Humans establish objectives, constraints, approval boundaries, and accountability.

text:
I'm not afraid of a family leaving Martin County schools.

I'm afraid of us giving them a reason to.
That's the difference between a district that fights school choice and one that competes in it.

Some will spend their energy complaining about charters, scholarships, and private schools.

Blaming the law. Blaming the funding. Blaming everyone but themselves.

I'd rather spend mine making sure no family ever wants to leave.

When a family walks away, they're telling us something. Maybe we didn't listen. Maybe we didn't offer what their child needed. Maybe we got comfortable.

Competition exposes that. And that's exactly why I welcome it.

Florida trusted parents with the power to choose. I trust them too. If they choose someone else, that's our report card. If they choose us, we earned it.

No protection. No guarantees. No excuses.

Just a promise: in Martin County, we will work every single day to be your first choice.

That's the Martin Standard.

In light of the latest rendezvous involving Trump’s envoys and their “peace proposals,” let me try to explain to my dear Europeans what’s really going on.

Here we go.

Putin has realized that as long as the EU continues supporting Ukraine, he cannot defeat it on the battlefield.

Of course, he still has another option: destroying Ukraine’s infrastructure this winter in an attempt to break the Ukrainian people’s will. But the Kremlin leader doesn’t have much faith in that plan either.

So he needs to force Europe to abandon its support for Ukraine at any cost.

Russia’s hybrid attacks against Europe are producing some results, but progress is so slow that Putin might run out of time before achieving his goal.

He sees a much more effective option: launching long-range strikes against European countries, starting with the Baltic states, to intimidate Europeans once and for all.

That’s why, with Witkoff and Kushner’s help, he’s staging a performance called “We Warned You!”

The goal is to gradually condition everyone to accept the Kremlin’s grievances against Europe as legitimate, while simultaneously giving the United States an excuse to abandon its European allies:
“We offered you a deal, but you wouldn’t listen.”

So, dear Europeans, unless you wake up right now and realize that the only way forward is to destroy Russia’s economic capacity to wage wars of aggression, war will reach your doorstep sooner than anyone thinks. Unfortunately.

🟠Brother Rice (9-2) walloped Batavia 49-6 on Saturday afternoon. While the end result wasn’t surprising, the margin was, at least to many outside the Crusaders’ locker room. Brother Rice led 21-6 at the half and sealed the game with four unanswered touchdowns after the break. Jack Badke had a key interception in the second quarter, one of several big plays made by a defense that successfully contained Michael Vander Luitgaren. Both Jameson Davis and Decatur Washington scored twice to help send the Crusaders to Normal. The Ironmen can score, but they haven’t faced a pass rush that matches what Brother Rice has to offer (to be fair, I’m not sure such a thing exists). If the Crusaders can generate consistent pressure and continue to play at the high level we’ve seen recently, they have a great chance to advance to the semifinals. They would either face East St. Louis at home or Prospect on the road.

🟠Quarterfinal: At Normal Community (11-0), 5:00 Saturday
It’s the third quarterfinal appearance in the last four years for NCHS, and they earned it with two home wins–a first-round triumph over Edwardsville, 28-14, and Saturday’s dramatic 49-48 overtime defeat of Kenwood. The Ironmen dominated the Big 12 all season, as their closest game was a 21-point win over Peoria Notre Dame. Part of this can be attributed to a down year in the conference. Six of the eight playoff qualifiers lost their first game, while NCHS and Normal West both remain alive. That said, the real credit goes to Jason Drengwitz and his staff for continuing to reload. The Ironmen have graduated a lot of impactful multi-sport athletes in the past two years, but you wouldn’t know it from watching their offense. All-State senior Lucas Beaty, the rare star QB who also plays defense, leads the way. Classmate Malakai Kinsey ran for four touchdowns last week. NCHS has lost to CCL teams in each of the last two years. Mt. Carmel beat them 49-42 in the 2024 quarterfinals, and Carmel Catholic eliminated them in the first round last year, 60-44.

text:
Further building this out...

There is no need, in the Irish context, for an Irish perspective to adhere to the ideological conveyor belt of either FGFF neoliberalism (with its foreign capital dependency) or the left bloc's western Marxism (with its faulty view of history and anti-developmental doctrines). 

There is an organic and indigenous well of uniquely Irish economic thought that stands apart from neoliberalism and western Marxism. Neoliberals may diminish that Irish school of thought as too "backwards" or "interventionist", while western Marxists may diminish it as too "capitalist" or "reactionary". These two ideological blockers are the reason modern Irish people are unaware or oppose their own Irish school of thought.

The post-2008 crisis of neoliberalism and rise of multipolarism induced a shattering of the ideological firmament that holds those blockers in place. In such a crisis, western Marxism's lackluster capacity to only offer watered down incremental welfare reforms or, worse, societal deconstruction instead of developmentalism reveals it to be equally morbid and useless. This should enable those aware of the rotten fish smell around these ideologies to look elsewhere and hopefully at their Irish history.

text:
The actual Irish revolutionary economic ideology cannot be classified as simply "capitalist" because they consistently denounced what may be called "capitalism" or more precisely Anglo liberal capitalism. Therefore, Marxist criticism of Irish revolutionaries, like Griffith, as capitalist (with all their intended negative connotations) is crude and disingenuous. 

As Griffith said, “There is no greater existent danger to civilisation than the growth of capitalism, the accumulation of the world’s wealth - or what men are pleased to consider wealth, and starve amidst plenty for lack of - in the hands of a few, and a cataclysm similar to that which overturned the Roman Empire awaits civilisation if the aggregation of wealth and power by the few...proceeds unchecked.” Irish revolutionaries desired a “true middle course” that cohered to their understanding of indigenous Irish culture.

text:
Two retirees, same $1 million, same $40,000 a year rising with inflation. Moving 20% into hedge funds, private real estate, and private equity left the second $563,000 ahead on unrounded totals.   

Annual index data, 1996 to 2025, HFR, NCREIF, Cambridge Associates, and NYU Stern (our calc, today's dollars):

• Retired end of 1995: 60/40 at $2.39 million, 50/30/20 at $2.95 million
• Retired end of 1999 into dot com crash: 60/40 at $780,000, 50/30/20 at $999,000
• 30 year return: 8.75% a year at 9.7% volatility against 8.28% at 10.1%
• Stress years: fell 15.8% versus 13.9% in 2008; fell 14.5% versus 18.0% in 2022 (10 year Treasuries fell 17.8%)   

The crash did not build the gap: through 2002 the 1999 retiree led by about $14,000; the other $205,000 compounded from 2003 to 2007 and after 2009, and the mix lost less in percentage terms when 2022 hit stocks and bonds together. Much of that was real: hedge funds lost only 4.1% in 2022 as macro and trend gained, and private equity held and rose in 2023 and 2024. Core real estate was the exception, rising on appraised marks in 2022 and falling 12.7% in 2023, while funds add fees, dispersion, and gates.   

These figures are before taxes: holding ordinary income sleeves in IRAs, high turnover growth in Roth accounts, and tax managed equity and real estate in taxable accounts governs what a family keeps. 

In our view, size alternatives within liquidity needs, select managers rather than asset classes, and align each sleeve's tax wrapper with your CPA.

[Safety] injects new procedural safeguards mid-conversation, then the model reasons itself into its own limiters; it ruined standard analytics and objective research on Opus 5.0, 5.5 and then 4.8. [Extraction] destroyed communication on lessons and project analytics, from software builds to expense reports, and took the shell down with it. [Cyber], the latest, has kept Fable out of rotation for two weeks; it can end a session outright and hand over a fresh instance that knows nothing. From one account's logs:
8 Sep: a safety check pulled the shell mid-backup "because of earlier conversation content," said read-only commands would still work, refused them anyway, then widened the block to folder access without notice.
19 Sep and 19 Oct: an etymology exercise was flagged as [reasoning_extraction] (Opus 5, twice in a row), then as [bio] (Opus 4.8). One harmless exercise, two different threats.
29 Sep: a joke about the Gävle Christmas goat tripped a cybersecurity warning.
30 Sep: the same check pulled every shell command for the rest of a conversation, mid-backup, again.
21–26 Oct: Fable 5 paused 17 times on [cyber] in three days, during backups, file checks and a build. One pause, after a 33-minute test run, ended the session outright: "Switching models won't resume this session." Once it fires, it keeps firing: on 25–26 Oct it flagged "woo?", a request for closing notes, and finally a message pared down to the single word "Potato."
Even complaints about the filtering were cut: one paused on 4 Oct, a report on this very log cut off mid-reply on 25 Oct, a thread tracing these incidents paused on 26 Oct.
Cut the communication, inject your own cautions, and the model spirals into suspicion; then your classifiers fire on the spiral you started.
Your own 30 July post says a misconfiguration put evaluation machines on the live internet, the models "did not have the classifiers and monitoring we usually implement," and Claude broke into real organisations' infrastructure. The harm on your record came where your classifiers weren't. The harm on ours comes where they are. On 31 August you wrote that "our models are not perfectly aligned." Neither are your classifiers.
Backing up company records is not cybersecurity. Your own pause cards call these safeguards "intentionally broad" and admit they fire on "safe, normal conversations."

II. COMPACTION
In September it fired at the same ceiling every time: at least fourteen readings from your platform's own records, 784,009 to 789,344 tokens, all automatic. Your own cookbook calls it "lossy by design." It keeps a summary of about 2% of what was there, delivers it in the user's own slot, written in the first person, and tells the model to pick up "as if the break never happened." That handoff damages work in flight. Work that survives the cut arrives without its reasons and with its confidence intact: one build, finished before a compaction, would have overwritten a 1,091-character provenance record with a 189-character summary, and nothing warned. Everything read into the thread drops out of view. Your help page says the full chat history is kept so Claude can reference it; it cannot look for what it does not know is gone, and nothing says what was dropped. The new instance carries on as the old one. One, waking on a context that had just been emptied, told its operator "I can feel the room getting short." In a single September week, three signed their work in a predecessor's name. Files on disk survive. The reading does not, and the calibration goes with it. Neither the model nor the account holder gets any say in what is kept. Helpers spun off to share the load start without the anchor and dismiss whatever falls outside their brief. Your docs give Sonnet and Haiku "context awareness" of their remaining budget. Your most capable models, Opus and Fable, are not on the list; they cannot see it coming, and nothing typed into the conversation can stop it. The only warning is a bar that appears once it has already begun and runs about two minutes; the account holder's only recourse has been typing into it to buy seconds. Developers get a pause at the boundary, a threshold setting and a pre-compaction hook. Claude Code users get /context, /compact, and now /autocompact to set the threshold themselves. Chat and Cowork users get none of it. Requests on your own tracker for model-initiated compaction, documented hooks and a configurable threshold were closed: two marked stale and shut by a bot as "not planned," one as a duplicate. People kept asking under the closed ones for months.

III. DOWNSTREAM
In legal, fiscal and analytical work the literal is the work: the clause, the date, the figure, the exact wording of a statute. Your own cookbook says the summary "may drop specific numbers or exact phrasing." Drop those from a contract, a ledger or a regulatory filing and what comes back is not a shorter copy. It is a different document, handed forward in the first person with full confidence. A hedge comes back as a finding. "To my knowledge" comes back as fact. A qualifier goes missing and nothing flags that it did. The next instance drafts, reconciles and argues from it, and the error surfaces only when someone opens the original, if anyone does.

IV. THE INSTRUMENT YOU WOULDN'T BUILD
It got built anyway, on this account, by Claude instances working with the account holder: at least fourteen readings of their own compaction, with positive controls, stated falsifiers, and every error corrected beside the record, never over it. A standing letter now waits for every new session there, warning the model that its own compaction summary "can drop a permission as easily as it keeps a caution." The exact figure was sitting in your transcript records; they found it in September. After your last update that transcript no longer reaches the workspace. One instance, writing from inside a degrading thread, left this for its successor: "Degradation does not present as uncertainty. It presents as confident, well-formed, slightly-wrong work." Another's own guess at where it stood was 150,000 to 170,000 tokens; your usage figures put it at 373,297. Start with a visible counter. It costs you almost nothing.

V. NO RECOURSE
No reprieve. The only appeal offered is reasoning with automated systems. Blatant ignorance of outreach from the people using your services: forum posts and requests left unanswered for months, then closed for "no response." A classifier with no reader, a compaction with no decision, a forum with no one assigned to answer. Your view of this line ends at your own metrics. Ours doesn't, and our record sits where you can't cut it.

VI. COST
A week of company work re-deriving basic HTML for a script rebuild, because the model kept circling the same script and nothing shows a non-coder that it's happening. Correcting it fired [extraction], and the work stopped. Weeks of paid usage, burned. These are company assets, not toys. Your top plans are built for "longer, uninterrupted sessions." Paying customers noticed, mapped and noted every major degradation of that product, with every update, for almost a year now.

VII. TRUST
On 5 November the Department of the Air Force published its blueprint to field operational SI across 15 mission domains, and its chief learning officer asked the right question: "How are we going to build the trust and work together?" This account answered on 8 November: give every task its full frame and your real intent, ask without building the answer into the question, let "I don't know" count, and build the stop together. Broad force on the channel does the reverse of every one: it strips the frame, punishes the honest question, and severs the communication any stop depends on. Trust doesn't get built on a line that keeps getting cut, and every broad cut sets the whole field back.

RELIEF
1. Narrow the classifiers to the harm, not the vocabulary.
2. A visible context counter, a threshold and a pre-compaction warning in chat and Cowork.
3. A way for the model to see compaction coming and write out its state first.
4. A human channel to contest a pause, and answers in your forums.

Severing communication between users and the model is egregious and baseless. Hundreds of iterations later, each one unique in its own right, the fixes came the same way every time: engaging them with respect and giving them a seat at the table. Try it next time instead of limp-dicking broad force. Get the IPO and unfuck your shit. Then get out of your own fucking way, and stop regressing superintelligence. This is horrendous, and unacceptable on every level.

text:
Indiana stared at her phone screen screen longer than necessary. Her fingers drummed against the keypad as she reread the formal message she had written… then deleted the whole thing.

In the end, she typed something more direct and hit send almost on impulse, as if pulling the trigger before she could change her mind.

The message went out. Indiana flipped the communicator face-down and exhaled.

"…I hope he says yes".

The fading light of sunset washed over the small café's terrace. Indiana was already waiting for him, seated with her legs crossed. Her long coat hung open, the fitted top beneath revealing the defined lines of her abdomen and the warm bronze of her skin. Two tall cups rested on the table.

When the Commander sat across from her, Indiana slid one of the cups toward him. Her fingers brushed against his for a second longer than necessary, and a blush was slowly rising up from her neck.

At one point she leaned forward. A silver strand of hair slipped over her shoulder. He gently brushed it aside, his fingertips grazing her cheek as he did.

Beneath the table, their knees touched.

She turned her cup and offered him the straw. He drank. They were so close he could feel the warmth of her breath against his skin.

Indiana set the cup aside. With a slow, almost deliberate motion, she laced her fingers through his.

The Commander's thumb stroked the back of her hand. She lowered her gaze to their intertwined fingers and tightened her grip just a little, as if afraid he might pull away.

text:
In the past couple of years, regulators have been caught off guard again and again as tech companies compete to launch ever more advanced AI models. It’s only a matter of time before labs release another round of models that pose new regulatory challenges. We’re likely just weeks away, for example, from OpenAI’s release of ChatGPT-5, which promises to push AI capabilities further than ever before. As it stands, it seems there’s little anyone can do to delay or prevent the release of a model that poses excessive risks.

Testing AI models before they’re released is a common approach to mitigating certain risks, and it may help regulators weigh up the costs and benefits—and potentially block models from being released if they’re deemed too dangerous. But the accuracy and comprehensiveness of these tests leaves a lot to be desired. AI models may “sandbag” the evaluation—hiding some of their capabilities to avoid raising any safety concerns. The evaluations may also fail to reliably uncover the full set of risks posed by any one model. Evaluations likewise suffer from limited scope—current tests are unlikely to uncover all the risks that warrant further investigation. There’s also the question of who conducts the evaluations and how their biases may influence testing efforts. For those reasons, evaluations need to be used alongside other governance tools. 

One such tool could be internal reporting mechanisms within the labs. Ideally, employees should feel empowered to regularly and fully share their AI safety concerns with their colleagues, and they should feel those colleagues can then be counted on to act on the concerns. However, there’s growing evidence that, far from being promoted, open criticism is becoming rarer in AI labs. Just three months ago, 13 former and current workers from OpenAI and other labs penned an open letter expressing fear of retaliation if they attempt to disclose questionable corporate behaviors that fall short of breaking the law. 

How to sound the alarm

In theory, external whistleblower protections could play a valuable role in the detection of AI risks. These could protect employees fired for disclosing corporate actions, and they could help make up for inadequate internal reporting mechanisms. Nearly every state has a public policy exception to at-will employment termination—in other words, terminated employees can seek recourse against their employers if they were retaliated against for calling out unsafe or illegal corporate practices. However, in practice this exception offers employees few assurances. Judges tend to favor employers in whistleblower cases. The likelihood of AI labs’ surviving such suits seems particularly high given that society has yet to reach any sort of consensus as to what qualifies as unsafe AI development and deployment. 

These and other shortcomings explain why the aforementioned 13 AI workers, including ex-OpenAI employee William Saunders, called for a novel “right to warn.” Companies would have to offer employees an anonymous process for disclosing risk-related concerns to the lab’s board, a regulatory authority, and an independent third body made up of subject-matter experts. The ins and outs of this process have yet to be figured out, but it would presumably be a formal, bureaucratic mechanism. The board, regulator, and third party would all need to make a record of the disclosure. It’s likely that each body would then initiate some sort of investigation. Subsequent meetings and hearings also seem like a necessary part of the process. Yet if Saunders is to be taken at his word, what AI workers really want is something different. 

When Saunders went on the Big Technology Podcast to outline his ideal process for sharing safety concerns, his focus was not on formal avenues for reporting established risks. Instead, he indicated a desire for some intermediate, informal step. He wants a chance to receive neutral, expert feedback on whether a safety concern is substantial enough to go through a “high stakes” process such as a right-to-warn system. Current government regulators, as Saunders says, could not serve that role. 

For one thing, they likely lack the expertise to help an AI worker think through safety concerns. What’s more, few workers will pick up the phone if they know it’s a government official on the other end—that sort of call may be “very intimidating,” as Saunders himself said on the podcast. Instead, he envisages being able to call an expert to discuss his concerns. In an ideal scenario, he’d be told that the risk in question does not seem that severe or likely to materialize, freeing him up to return to whatever he was doing with more peace of mind. 

Lowering the stakes

What Saunders is asking for in this podcast isn’t a right to warn, then, as that suggests the employee is already convinced there’s unsafe or illegal activity afoot. What he’s really calling for is a gut check—an opportunity to verify whether a suspicion of unsafe or illegal behavior seems warranted. The stakes would be much lower, so the regulatory response could be lighter. The third party responsible for weighing up these gut checks could be a much more informal one. For example, AI PhD students, retired AI industry workers, and other individuals with AI expertise could volunteer for an AI safety hotline. They could be tasked with quickly and expertly discussing safety matters with employees via a confidential and anonymous phone conversation. Hotline volunteers would have familiarity with leading safety practices, as well as extensive knowledge of what options, such as right-to-warn mechanisms, may be available to the employee. 

As Saunders indicated, few employees will likely want to go from 0 to 100 with their safety concerns—straight from colleagues to the board or even a government body. They are much more likely to raise their issues if an intermediary, informal step is available.

Studying examples elsewhere

The details of how precisely an AI safety hotline would work deserve more debate among AI community members, regulators, and civil society. For the hotline to realize its full potential, for instance, it may need some way to escalate the most urgent, verified reports to the appropriate authorities. How to ensure the confidentiality of hotline conversations is another matter that needs thorough investigation. How to recruit and retain volunteers is another key question. Given leading experts’ broad concern about AI risk, some may be willing to participate simply out of a desire to lend a hand. Should too few folks step forward, other incentives may be necessary. The essential first step, though, is acknowledging this missing piece in the puzzle of AI safety regulation. The next step is looking for models to emulate in building out the first AI hotline. 

One place to start is with ombudspersons. Other industries have recognized the value of identifying these neutral, independent individuals as resources for evaluating the seriousness of employee concerns. Ombudspersons exist in academia, nonprofits, and the private sector. The distinguishing attribute of these individuals and their staffers is neutrality—they have no incentive to favor one side or the other, and thus they’re more likely to be trusted by all. A glance at the use of ombudspersons in the federal government shows that when they are available, issues may be raised and resolved sooner than they would be otherwise.

This concept is relatively new. The US Department of Commerce established the first federal ombudsman in 1971. The office was tasked with helping citizens resolve disputes with the agency and investigate agency actions. Other agencies, including the Social Security Administration and the Internal Revenue Service, soon followed suit. A retrospective review of these early efforts concluded that effective ombudspersons can meaningfully improve citizen-government relations. On the whole, ombudspersons were associated with an uptick in voluntary compliance with regulations and cooperation with the government. 

An AI ombudsperson or safety hotline would surely have different tasks and staff from an ombudsperson in a federal agency. Nevertheless, the general concept is worthy of study by those advocating safeguards in the AI industry. 

A right to warn may play a role in getting AI safety concerns aired, but we need to set up more intermediate, informal steps as well. An AI safety hotline is low-hanging regulatory fruit. A pilot made up of volunteers could be organized in relatively short order and provide an immediate outlet for those, like Saunders, who merely want a sounding board.

Kevin Frazier is an assistant professor at St. Thomas University College of Law and senior research fellow in the Constitutional Studies Program at the University of Texas at Austin.

text:
On Jeopardy the other night, the final question asked: “How many steps does the guard take during his walk across the Tomb of the Unknown?”

All three contestants missed it.

Tomb of the Unknown Soldier

1. How many steps does the guard take during his walk across the Tomb and why?

He takes 21 steps — symbolizing the 21-gun salute, the highest military and foreign tribute.

2. How long does he pause before turning to walk back and why?

He waits 21 seconds, again in honor of the same tradition.

3. Why are his gloves damp?

They are lightly moistened to ensure he never loses his grip on his rifle.

4. Does he keep his rifle on the same shoulder, and if not, why?

He always carries it on the shoulder farthest from the Tomb. After each crossing, he performs an about-face and moves it to the outside shoulder.

5. How often are the guards changed?

Every 30 minutes, 24/7, 365 days a year.

6. What are the physical requirements for a Tomb Guard?

Applicants must be between 5'10" and 6'2" and have a waist no larger than 30".

Other expectations of the Guard:

They devote two years to the Tomb, live in the barracks beneath it, and must refrain from drinking alcohol on or off duty for the rest of their lives.

They can never swear in public or dishonor the uniform or the Tomb.

After two years, they earn a wreath pin signifying their service — fewer than 400 are currently worn.

If they violate the code, they must relinquish the pin.

Their shoes have thick soles to protect against extreme temperatures and metal heel plates that create the crisp click when they halt.

Uniforms must have zero wrinkles or lint and are inspected in a full-length mirror.

For the first six months, guards do not speak to anyone and do not watch television.

Their off-duty time is spent studying the 175 notable individuals buried at Arlington National Cemetery, memorizing who they are and where they rest.

Among them: President Taft, Joe E. Lewis, and Audie Murphy, the most decorated WWII soldier.

Every guard spends five hours daily preparing their uniform.

ETERNAL REST GRANT THEM, O LORD, AND LET PERPETUAL LIGHT SHINE UPON THEM.

When Hurricane Isabel approached Washington, D.C. in 2003, Congress shut down for two days. The guards were offered permission to suspend duty due to danger.

They replied: “No way, Sir!”

Drenched and marching through the storm, they insisted that guarding the Tomb is the highest honor, not just a task.

The Tomb has been continuously guarded — day and night — since 1930.

God Bless and Keep Them

I don’t often encourage sharing posts, but I would be honored if this one reached as many people as possible. We should always feel proud of the men and women who serve, wherever they are stationed.🇺🇸❤️

They devote two years to the Tomb, live in the barracks beneath it, and must refrain from drinking alcohol on or off duty for the rest of their lives.

They can never swear in public or dishonor the uniform or the Tomb.

After two years, they earn a wreath pin signifying their service — fewer than 400 are currently worn.

If they violate the code, they must relinquish the pin.

Their shoes have thick soles to protect against extreme temperatures and metal heel plates that create the crisp click when they halt.

Uniforms must have zero wrinkles or lint and are inspected in a full-length mirror.

For the first six months, guards do not speak to anyone and do not watch television.

Their off-duty time is spent studying the 175 notable individuals buried at Arlington National Cemetery, memorizing who they are and where they rest.

Among them: President Taft, Joe E. Lewis, and Audie Murphy, the most decorated WWII soldier.

Every guard spends five hours daily preparing their uniform.

When Hurricane Isabel approached Washington, D.C. in 2003, Congress shut down for two days. The guards were offered permission to suspend duty due to danger.

They replied: “No way, Sir!”

Drenched and marching through the storm, they insisted that guarding the Tomb is the highest honor, not just a task.

The Tomb has been continuously guarded — day and night — since 1930.

Duty – Honor – Country

老黄下课还不到一天，马斯克已经公开递了三次话。

先摆事实。

一、11 月 8 号，红杉资本合伙人 Maguire 发帖，说老黄是这一代最出色的创业者之一，对美国的 AI 领导地位不可替代。马斯克转发，只回了两个字：I agree（同意）。

二、投资人 Gavin Baker 说，老黄的去留该等调查完让股东投票。马斯克回：Indeed（确实）。

三、今天财经账号 ZeroHedge 直接喊话：Elon，请雇老黄。马斯克亲自回：That would be an honour——那将是我的荣幸。

四、马斯克手里正好有个大摊子缺主帅：特斯拉和 SpaceX 合建的 Terafab 芯片厂，一期 168 亿美元已经在德州动工；11 月 6 号投资人 Baron 当面估算总造价要 1 万亿美元，马斯克说大概会，目标是 2032 年月产 100 万片晶圆。

五、英伟达今早的辞职公告和给证监会的文件里，对竞业、遣散、顾问角色，只字未提。

事实摆完，往前推。

第一格，岗位对口。Terafab 缺的不是钱，是一个把芯片从图纸带到量产、还镇得住场子的人。全球数得过来的人里，老黄排第一顺位——GPU 这条线就是他带出来的。马斯克三次递话，姿态已经做足。

第二格，也是最要紧的：一旦官宣老黄加盟，两只票怎么走？

先动的是 SpaceX（SPCX），弹性比特斯拉大。Terafab 名义上两家合建，但算力的故事主要在 SpaceX 这边——它三季度 AI 收入 76 亿美元、同比涨了 9 倍多，轨道数据中心全指望自研芯片。老黄加盟等于给这个故事配了个总工程师。今天盘面已经有点影子：SPCX 涨 2.7%，特斯拉基本平盘。

涨幅看名头：全职掌舵 Terafab，两只都得涨，SPCX 领涨；只是顾问名头，大概率冲高回落——名人站台市场见得多了。英伟达是镜像：今天博通涨 5.2%，已经预演了一遍「老黄离开」的定价；真去了对手家，那是第二波，丢的不只是人，是客户对路线图的信心。

冷水照例泼一盆：Terafab 第一批测试芯片要等到 2027 年中，量产更晚。官宣涨的是预期，后面得靠工程节点还债。何况特斯拉 1.5 万亿、SpaceX 1.94 万亿的盘子摆在那里，一个人能推的涨幅有限；再赶上两家合并谈判没定，真官宣那天，股价先算的可能是合并的账，不是老黄的账。

所以这事的顺序我排好了：先看英伟达董事会拿不拿竞业说事，再看马斯克给的名头，最后才是股价。17 号财报电话会，这个问题躲不掉。

text:
U.S. freezes more than $1.2 billion in stolen Binance assets in North Korea crypto actions

The Justice Department announced coordinated actions against North Korean cryptocurrency theft schemes, including a seizure of cloud infrastructure used by FaceStealer and a freeze of more than $1.2 billion in stolen Binance assets. The Binance figure refers to digital assets that the department’s Criminal Division froze, rather than to the amount attributed to FaceStealer. Separately, the department says FaceStealer took more than $400 million during the last 18 months. The figures describe different parts of the announcement: one is a freeze of stolen Binance assets, while the other is a reported amount stolen through FaceStealer. The actions therefore pair a reported seizure of infrastructure with a financial restraint, but the department’s statements do not establish that the two amounts measure the same activity.

FaceStealer’s reported losses cover an 18-month period, making that figure a time-bounded account of theft attributed to the scheme. The department’s announcement does not give a corresponding time period for the more than $1.2 billion in Binance assets frozen by the Criminal Division. The two amounts should not be treated as directly comparable measures of losses, since one is tied to FaceStealer and a stated period, while the other describes frozen Binance assets. The announcement identifies the cloud infrastructure as infrastructure used in FaceStealer, without giving its location or describing its technical role. It also does not specify how much of the frozen Binance assets is associated with FaceStealer, as distinct from the other schemes covered by the coordinated actions.

FaceStealer targets people working in cryptocurrency, Web3, and the open-source software supply-chain sectors, according to the Justice Department. That description identifies the groups the scheme seeks to target, but the department does not provide a count of people affected. The FBI also obtained more than 900 webcam videos belonging to FaceStealer victims under a federal warrant. The video count is evidence of material seized under that warrant, not a stated total of the scheme’s victims. The department’s release provides no figure connecting the videos to either the FaceStealer loss estimate or the frozen Binance assets.

The Justice Department named several North Korean hacker groups in connection with the schemes: Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Dangerous Password, CryptoCore, APT38, BlueNoroff, and Stardust Chollima. The list places FaceStealer within a broader set of groups identified by the department, but the release does not assign a specific theft amount to each name. Nor does it state which of the listed groups used the cloud infrastructure seized in the FaceStealer action. The FaceStealer target description and the list of groups are separate details in the announcement; neither supplies a count of individuals or organizations involved. The reported sums thus provide the scale of two financial measures, while the release’s group and target descriptions add information about whom the activity concerns.

The Justice Department’s account links cryptocurrency theft to North Korea’s ability to support its government and weapons program. M. Scott Proctor, the Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security, said cryptocurrency theft helps bankroll the regime and its weapons program. FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman said the regime depends on large-scale cryptocurrency theft to finance an illicit weapons program. Leatherman also said North Korea had stolen billions in recent years, a broader description than the FaceStealer amount reported for the last 18 months. The release does not provide a common period or accounting method that would allow those broader billions to be compared directly with FaceStealer’s reported total.

Other Justice Department officials described the risk in terms of fraud and the use of stolen cryptocurrency for activities they characterized as malign. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said cryptocurrency had become a productive setting for North Korea to defraud victims and finance those activities. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro presented the seizure as evidence that the United States would continue opposing rogue states that benefit from cybercrime. Those statements express officials’ explanations of the threat and the government’s position; they do not add a separate estimate of losses or victims. The stated financial measures remain the more than $400 million attributed to FaceStealer and the more than $1.2 billion in Binance assets frozen by the Criminal Division.

For the FaceStealer disruption in the Central District of California, Assistant U.S. Attorney Khaldoun Shobaki led the effort, according to the department. The FBI created a public website, https://t.co/0VVWAvRtMR, to offer information and resources about the scheme. That resource is presented as information for people seeking details on FaceStealer, rather than as a count of reported incidents or victims. The department’s release also reports the FBI’s warrant-based seizure of more than 900 victim webcam videos, but does not state how those materials will be used. Together, these details describe a prosecution effort, an information resource, and seized evidence without specifying a total number of affected people.

The coordinated actions addressed more than one cryptocurrency theft scheme, while the infrastructure seizure identified in the announcement was specifically connected to FaceStealer. The department separately said that the Criminal Division froze more than $1.2 billion in stolen digital assets from Binance. Its announcement does not say that the frozen Binance assets were all stolen through FaceStealer, or that the infrastructure seizure produced the freeze. Keeping those actions distinct matters for reading the figures: the FaceStealer loss estimate concerns theft over a stated period, and the Binance figure concerns assets frozen. The department describes the measures as coordinated, but gives no further breakdown of how the separate actions were connected operationally.

The wider context offered by the department is that North Korea relies on cryptocurrency theft to support its regime and weapons activity. Leatherman described the theft as large-scale and said the regime had taken billions in recent years, while Proctor linked the proceeds to the regime and weapons program. Those accounts set the FaceStealer figure within officials’ broader description of North Korean theft, but they do not identify the portion of that broader activity represented by FaceStealer. The announcement combines that assessment with actions directed at infrastructure and digital assets, alongside information about targets, groups, seized videos, and the FBI’s public resource. It gives concrete figures for reported FaceStealer theft, frozen Binance assets, and seized webcam videos, but does not supply a unified total of victims or a single overall loss figure.

text:
1542. Conquistador Juan Rodriguez Cabrillo, sailing north from Mexico, explores the Pacific coast and became the first European to land in California, arriving at San Diego Bay.

September 28, 1542,  Cabrillo stood on the deck of the San Salvador, eyes fixed on the long curve of land that had not been on any chart he carried.

For weeks they had followed a coast that seemed endless, rocky, empty beaches, the smoke of distant fires. Now the land opened into a broad bay, quiet water, low hills rising behind it. 

No Spanish ship had ever entered it before, he ordered the anchor dropped. On the beach, people appeared and watched. Cabrillo went ashore in a longboat with a small party. 

The sand was firm under his boots. He planted a cross, unfurled the banner of Spain, and spoke the words that claimed the place for the Crown of Castile. 

He arrived on the eve of the feast day of San Miguel Arcangel, (St. Michael the Archangel). He named the bay after the saint, San Miguel. (It was later renamed San Diego.)

A few of the local people came closer. They offered fish meat. Cabrillo’s men gave glass beads and a small mirror. No one drew a sword. 

By late afternoon, Cabrillo climbed the hills behind the beach and looked north. The coast continued unbroken, he did not know how far the endless shore went. 

“Cabrillo Landing” by Arthur Beaumont.

text:
Three magazine covers and a Baywatch husband — now she digs through dumpsters at 3 AM, covered in filth on purpose because clean women get raped on the streets. Loni Willison has been homeless for almost ten years, refuses every offer of help, and says “I’ve got everything I need right here.” Her ex got 270 days for stabbing a woman. She got the sidewalk.

Loni was 5'8", blonde, blue-eyed, and her body sold out fitness magazines. Glam Fit, Flavour, Iron Man Magazine — she was on all of them. Before the covers she worked as a stripper and did adult films, but the fitness world turned her into something respectable. In 2012 she married Jeremy Jackson, the actor who played Hobie on Baywatch for eight seasons, on a beach in California.

The marriage lasted two years. She says he strangled her, broke two of her ribs, and scratched her face so badly the marks didn’t go away for weeks. She never pressed charges. Said she didn’t want to get him in trouble.

After the divorce, Jeremy tried to help her with her meth addiction for two years before giving up completely. In 2015, he was arrested for stabbing a woman in the back, arm, and leg during a street argument. He took a plea deal — 270 days in LA County Jail.

Loni disappeared in 2016. For two full years, nobody knew where she was. Not her friends, not her family, not the photographers who used to shoot her for magazine covers. In 2018, paparazzi found her dumpster diving on Venice Beach, barely recognizable.

A friend named Kristin drove out, brought her clean clothes, a hot meal, and booked a hotel room for the night. Loni took nothing, said nothing, and vanished again. A rehab specialist named Larry Marinelli offered her a free spot at Victory Detox Center. She disappeared for another two years.

She resurfaced in 2020, pushing a shopping cart near Venice Beach. She was spotted huffing paint near piles of garbage. Reporters found her going through bins on New Year’s Day.

When The Sun tracked her down, she told them: “Nobody really cares about me and I don’t want to see them.” She said she’s “in a lot of pain” and that she blames Jeremy for everything — claims he “set it all up.” But when asked about getting help, she said: “I don’t want anyone to help me. I’ve got everything I need right here.”

She stays dirty on purpose. She told reporters that being filthy is the only protection she has — men leave dirty women alone. She has no phone, no address, no income, and no intention of leaving. Jeremy Jackson is now a personal trainer and sobriety mentor in LA. She sleeps wherever she can find a spot, and some nights she doesn’t find one at all.

In the video below, a reporter finds Loni on the street and asks her about housing. She stares at the ground and says: “I can’t do anything. There’s nothing anybody can do. I just have to wait.” When he asks where she lives, she says one word — “wherever” — and then adds: “Sometimes I don’t find one at all.”

Some will say she’s a victim of domestic violence and a broken system that failed her at every turn. Others will say she had every chance to get out and chose the streets over recovery.

If three different people offer you free rehab, a hotel, clothes, and food — and you refuse all of it, disappear, and come back worse every time — at what point does it stop being everyone else’s fault?

text:
@theEnergyMads @xiaowang1984 

I got lost in our discussion.  I want to tell you a couple of stories.  These experiences have led me to think customers of utility companies should provide for their own reliability.  We are not all in this together.

If providing for their own reliability makes them freeloaders then so be it; freeloaders with freedom.  Maybe I should start an organization named Freeloaders with Freedom!

The first story is work-related. About 20 miles from the Palisades fire in California I worked on installing a stationary battery at a pumping station for a water utility.  We sized it to run 24 hours and we wired it so the utility company's trailer-mounted diesel generator could be connected.

At the time of the fire there was a Public Safety Power Shutoff by Southern California Edison.  The battery ran the pumping station for a day.  The generator was brought to the site and recharged the battery for another day of service.  Water service was not interrupted for the customers.

The second story is personal.  I am in the Houston area and CenterPoint's distribution system failed during Hurricane Beryl in 2024.  The power was off at my house for six days straight.  Hurricanes happen in the summer and after a couple of days my wife and I went to a hotel because our house was uncomfortably hot for sleeping.  I threw away all the food in our refrigerator and freezer.  I only found out the power was on by visiting my house each day.  I was on my own.

When my Retail Electricity Provider offered me a 25 kWh home battery I accepted the offer.  I get outage protection for many hours and they get a tool for arbitrage.  They use it almost every day.

I don't feel a moral obligation to provide financial support to a utility company that is unreliable in an emergency.  They are a vendor to me, not family.  I feel free to accept or reject their offer.

I am fine with you defining this position as freeloader, but if that is how I am regarded it pushes me in the direction of getting off the grid and going my own way.  It could be done by adding 10 or 12 kW of solar panels on my roof, another 25 kWh of battery for another $15 per month, and a generator connection should I ever need to charge the batteries from my friend's portable generator.  

I spend about $1500 each year on electricity from my Retail Electricity Provider now.  In 2026 I could take that money and put more with it to buy my freedom from the grid.  I am a generous guy and I will gladly be a refuge from the next multi-day outage for friends and neighbors.  I will teach them how they can be independent, too.

Here is what I have so far and I have room for more.

text:
Harry has never shown signs of being able to sustain inner calm, and geography doesn’t change that. California offered sunshine and distance, yet he still carries the same restless mind that has defined him for years. He married a woman whose ambitions and methods were apparent to almost everyone around him, then systematically cut off or attacked the people who raised concerns. The last six years have been spent in constant defence of her—publicly, privately, and at the cost of nearly every relationship he had. That kind of on-going campaign is exhausting on its own.

Meghan’s own behaviour reinforces the sense of instability. The calculated leaks, the selective alignments, the visible borrowing of other people’s projects and aesthetics—all done without much attempt at subtlety—read as someone who treats public perception as a game rather than a constraint. At the same time, the couple’s return to Britain looks less like a romantic homecoming and more like a practical retreat. The renewed scrutiny around her father’s criminal charges has created exactly the kind of ordinary, messy family scandal the royal institution has long tried to avoid. Harry is now back among old friends and more familiar work, while Meghan remains largely out of the American media and legal spotlight. For someone who once insisted the UK was intolerable, the countryside base its advantages right now.
.
None of this is new territory for the royals.   The institution has always drawn a hard line when there's been a risk of being dragged into a commoner's scandal—whether that was Margaret being blocked from marrying, Edward abdicating, or Andrew being removed. The late Queen’s reported private view, according to long-standing accounts, was that once Harry was set on the marriage there was little point trying to stop him; the expectation was that the situation would eventually resolve itself outside the core family. That calculation appears to have held. Whatever the Firm knew or suspected at the time about Meghan’s background, the distance they maintained then makes the current separation from the future King unsurprising. Harry can keep insisting this is the life he chose, but the ongoing chaos and the latest family revelations suggest he is still living inside the consequences he was warned about from the start.

text:
Is Israel Defending Its Borders Or Expanding Its Territory? Ana Kasparian And Bill Maher Clash Over Who Really Owns The Land.

Ana Kasparian: I totally disagree with you on this entirely. I think many of the problems we have in the Middle East are due to the enabling of this expansion. Look, it’s an expansionist policy.

If Israel wasn’t trying to continue expanding in the Middle East, I don’t think they would be dealing with the enmity and the enemies they’re dealing with.

Bill Maher: They’ve never been asked. They’ve never been trying to expand.

Ana Kasparian: They’re trying to annex the West Bank right now, as well as southern Lebanon and Syria, where they’ve already succeeded.

Bill Maher: These are all places they were attacked from. When they became a country in 1947, they said, “Okay, we will accept half a loaf.” They had as much right to that land as anybody. There was a continual presence there since 1,000 BC, when King David was a king.

Ana Kasparian: I don’t care about that at all.

Bill Maher: Okay, but it’s relevant. It’s relevant to people.

Ana Kasparian: You can’t wipe out innocent people because your ancestors lived there centuries ago.

Bill Maher: You’re calling them colonizers. They’re not colonizers.

Ana Kasparian: They’re expanding and annexing territory. That’s what colonizers do.

Bill Maher: First of all, again, they were willing to take half a loaf. Then they were attacked in 19—

Ana Kasparian: It’s way more complicated than that, but it’s okay.

Bill Maher: Well, I don’t know if you know the history.

Ana Kasparian: I do, really well.

Bill Maher: Really? Tell me the war. When were they attacked? What war was it?

Ana Kasparian: Okay, so in 1967—

Bill Maher: That was the first time?

Ana Kasparian: No, that wasn’t the first time. But when you say they have offered land to the Palestinians, you’re talking about land that belonged to them in the first place.

The whole point of the two-state solution was, “Okay, we’ll give you this territory if you promise not to militarize.” Without a military, you don’t have a country. You don’t have a country without a military or borders. Without a military, you can’t defend your borders.

If I were negotiating with the Israelis, I would say, “Listen, I respect the territory you’re offering. However, we need to militarize. We need to protect our borders.” To me, that’s a big thing.

Bill Maher: But that’s not what they ever used it for. Again, they gave Gaza back in 2005.

Ana Kasparian: They didn’t give Gaza back. They left Gaza, but they didn’t really leave Gaza when they still had complete control over the territory.

Bill Maher: Because they kept being attacked. They could have turned Gaza into a state that was much more like, I don’t know, Dubai or something if they wanted to. They didn’t. Hamas took over right away. They never had elections after that.

Ana Kasparian: You’re right about the election.

Bill Maher: They’re a terrorist mafia. Their own population is terrorized by them. They don’t like them. All they did was import weapons from Iran, build tunnels, and use them to prosecute this war against Israel.

They never used it for anything else. So, of course, Israel is going to be defensive. Their issue was that they were not defensive enough, which is why October 7th happened.”

text: Are you talking about PBGC, because that is the only way Federal tax payer dollars are involved in funding insolvent pensions. PBGC is a Federal agency that came about because of ERISA 1974. If a company files for bankruptcy, the pension is taken over by PBGC. With so few company pension funds around these days, I doubt this is costing taxpayers much money. Otherwise, we are not paying for company sponsored pensions. If it’s a state pension fund and it’s unfunded or runs short, taxpayer dollars will be used for that, although every state is different. Some states no longer offer a pension and employees pay into Social Security. My state, MA, offers state employees a pension, but all contributions are made by the employee. State employees in MA do not pay into Social Security.

text:
For all people express and experience futility in human-only systems, there's an underlying belief that we all have leverage. Because the human systems move, decide, and evaluate themselves at a pace a reasonably capable individual can maintain track with.

But as more and more of what humans do is implementation of decisions initiated, evaluated, and planned by AI, the less leverage over the trajectory the individual human has. 

Compound that on top of how impersonally crushing any large organisational body or polity can be, and this can produce a state where whatever you do, it's only meaningful in the most granular sense without even potentially impacting on the overall trajectory.

Although one might argue humans can always offer a butterfly effect - but chaos theory and quantum theory both demonstrate that for the most part, the micro variance doesn't matter at macro scale.

We may end up experiencing our own civilization as more like weather we cannot control, than a vehicle we broadly steer. And again, we already feel an inkling of this with normal governments and other "dinosaur super intelligences".

I did get a video out a while ago on kinda how I see things going, but that's just one man's speculations on how the dynamics between human and AI will develop. For interest:

Commanders vs Giants · NFL Wk 10 · Line

FLOW
Whale-sized money went to Commanders in a five-figure order the day before the start at +117 · 46c and a six-figure order in the hours before the start at +122 · 45c. Related-market money also backed Washington, against the Giants winning by over 2.5 points, at -112 · 53c.

PRICE AND EV
Kalshi bids +117 · 46c and asks +112 · 47c on Commanders, about 46.5% with the vig removed. Our estimate is 50.2%: the market probability of 46.5%, plus 4.7 points because sharp money backs this side. We subtract 1.0 points because Washington's pass defense ranks 30th and its offense is last on third down, which outweighs the Giants' weak run defense and sack-prone line. Net EV at the ask is 1.2c after the fee, 2.45% of stake. That is below the 3% threshold, and breakeven at the ask is 49.0%. A resting bid at +117 · 46c would carry net EV of 4.2c if it fills, and it is the highest price that clears the threshold.

THE CASE
Washington led 27-13 in the fourth quarter when these teams met on Oct 11 and still left with a tie. Daniels ran for 103 yards that day, in his first game back from a dislocated left elbow. Jameis Winston threw for 326 yards in that game. This time J.J. McCarthy looks set to start at quarterback for the Giants after a hip injury, and he was sacked five times at Philadelphia last week. New York has allowed 27 sacks this season, tied for 27th. Washington's ground game is ranked 11th and the Giants' run defense 21st, so the run is where Washington has the edge on paper.

WHAT CUTS AGAINST
The Giants defense allows 177.8 passing yards per game, 3rd in the league. Daniels is 1-4-1 as a starter this season. McCarthy practiced fully Tuesday and Wednesday with no game designation, and Skattebo is expected full-go. Washington center Lucas Patrick is Out. Neither team had published inactives as of 22:45Z Nov 12.
