text:
While we're on the subject of the great Gerardo Gonzalez, aka Kid Gavilan, he still had enough left in the tank to score a ten-round unanimous decsion over the always tough Chico Vejar, at the Olympic Auditorium in Los Angeles, on November 13, 1956.

Both judges, Charley Randolph and Dynamite Jackson (Yep, you've read that name here before), scored it lopsided in favor of "The Cuban Hawk" as did referee Mushy Callahan (I know we have covered him here as well).

2-5-1 in his previous eight bouts, this win would be only a delay of the inevitable slippage and spin the Kid was in the midst of; he'd lose his next five bouts, and he dropped eight of his final eleven fights.
----------------------------------------------------------
Isidoro Francisco "Chico" Vejar, known during the early part of his career as “Stamford’s Socking Schoolboy", was one of the most popular TV fighters of the 1950's. He was also one of the better boxers to never win a world title.

From Boxing24/7:

"America started watching television in the late 1940’s, and the Friday Night fights were broadcast weekly by Gillette and Pabst Blue Ribbon from the late ‘40s into the early 1960’s. Back when Don Dunphy was commentator, fights like Hairston vs. Keogh, Satterfield vs. Brothers, Rosi vs. Compo, and Castellani vs. Durando thrilled TV audiences everywhere, but no one seemed to fight more often or was more popular than Chico Vejar. If the ‘50s were a wonderful stew of boxing, Chico was clearly part of the meat.” 
Bert Randolph Sugar once said “Chico Vejar was served up as much on Friday nights as fish was.”
Vejar, born in Stamford, Connecticut, was the world’s fifth-ranked middleweight by 1958. He fought 11 times at Madison Square Garden and appeared frequently in nationally televised fights. He also studied drama at New York University and appeared in two movies in the 1950’s that starred Tony Curtis and Audie Murphy ("World in My Corner" released in 1958 was one of them).
He'd have wins over Vince Martinez, Fitzie Pruden and Billy Graham but the closest he ever got to a title shot was an "elimination bout' 1st round TKO loss to Tony DeMarco in 1955.
Vejar would retire young, only 29, to care for a son with cerebral palsy. His son, tragically, would die in 1962 at three years old from complications of the disease.
Vejar would serve as executive director of both the Fairfield and Westchester county chapters of the United Cerebral Palsy Association and as a member of the Connecticut State Athletic Commission. He helped establish the Jimmy Vejar Day Camp in Rye Brook, N.Y. for children with cerebral palsy.
Trained by Whitey Bimstein, 92-20-4 (43 KO's) as a pro, Vejar died in 2016 at the age of 85.
---------------------------------------------------------
Mushy Callahan, now there's a boxing name if I ever heard one, you don't meet too many doctors or lawyers named 'Mushy Callahan', was well known in his latter years as a trainer of actors portraying boxers on film.
Among the actors Mushy Callahan trained for films were Montgomery Clift (From Here to Eternity), James Dean (Rebel Without a Cause), Kirk Douglas (Champion), Errol Flynn (Gentleman Jim), James Earl Jones (The Great White Hope), Burt Lancaster (Jim Thorpe – All-American), Anthony Quinn (Requiem for a Heavyweight), and Elvis Presley (Kid Galahad).
Mushy Callahan, born Vincent Morris Scheer in New York City, held the (NBA) World  Junior Welterweight Championship from September of 1926 to February of 1930.
Recognition at time was disputed. The Wisconsin Boxing Commission recognized Pinky Mitchell while others recognized James Herring and others would recognize the title vacant or not at all. Of course, as we have gone into before here, the junior welterweight division had an odd, and oft-disrupted, path to eventual universal recognition as a legitimate weight class.
Callahan acted in, and served as a boxing technical assistant on a number of boxing movies. He trained Elvis Presley for his role in Kid Galahad and also portrayed the referee in the movie's final climatic bout.
Callahan finished his own boxing career at 49-15-3 with 22 KO wins.
He was inducted into the World Boxing Hall of Fame posthumously in 1989.
From The Jewish Boxing Blog:
Mushy Callahan held the junior welterweight world championship for nearly three and a half years and after his boxing career ended, he trained the biggest Hollywood stars on the sets of their movies. Yet among fans of Jewish boxing, Callahan isn't revered like Benny Leonard nor is he admired like Barney Ross. 
Though his championship reign was long, it was hampered by several factors: the "synthetic" nature of his crown, his losses in over-the-weight bouts, and his propensity to duck the toughest challengers. His conversion to Catholicism after his career also contributed to Callahan's fallen star within the Jewish boxing community.
Vincent Morris Scheer was born on November 3, 1904 in New York to Jewish Austrian parents named Max and Anna. The family moved across the country to Los Angeles and settled in Boyle Heights when Vincent, who was known as Moishele, was two years old. Max sold produce near the intersection of Brooklyn Ave and Soto. Meanwhile, young Moishele got into a lot of fights. He resented when other kids called him "Maurice" and had no problem showing them with his fists. After a while, no one wanted to call him Maurice anymore, so he soon developed the nickname of Mushy, which would stick for the rest of his life. As a youngster, he worked as a newsboy, a profession that required boys to fight each other for access to the best corners.
At the age of ten, Scheer joined the Main Street Gym, which was also known as the Newsboys' Club. He fought in a lot of smokers and took the surname Callahan from a local fight promoter. His childhood friend, future Olympic gold medalist and two-time world champion Jackie Fields (we covered him just yesterday), remembered, "Mushy Callahan was the greatest. We were raised together selling papers. But he was always the big shot."
Once evening, Fields wanted Mushy to get him tickets to a show at the Orpheum. "When I asked him to get me two tickets he said, 'Get in line, you punk you.' So we almost had a fight on the street," Fields said.
Callahan turned pro in 1923 and quickly became a hot prospect. The next year, he dropped a couple of decisions to Johnny Adams, a very popular fighter in Los Angeles who was good, but not great. Callahan didn't hit many other bumps in the road on his climb to the top, though. He beat a quality veteran in Red Herring, took two ten-round decisions from former lightweight world champion Jimmy Goodrich, and went 1-0-1 against a world class opponent named Ace Hudkins.
(Me: We have discussed Hudkins here a few times. he was quite the interesting character himself!)
The first fight against Hudkins, which took place on September 16, 1925, was one of the most exciting battles in L.A. that year. Most observers felt referee Larry McGrath's decision to call it a draw was fair, but Callahan and his team vehemently disagreed. Willie Goldstein, who worked Callahan's corner, climbed through the ropes and attacked McGrath, receiving a hard left hook from the ref in return. Callahan and his manager E.W. Sears were both fined and suspended until December. McGrath was also suspended. Goldstein was banned for life.
Callahan won the rematch and then took the two fights against Goodrich. He was extremely popular among fight fans in Los Angeles. His July 5, 1926 fight against Jack Silver, a fan favorite from San Francisco, was billed as a clash between Southern California and Northern California. Coincidentally, Silver, like Callahan, was a Jewish fighter who would convert to Catholicism, work in Hollywood after his boxing career was done, and have a long and distinguished career as a referee.
In one of the biggest fights in California since bouts of over four rounds were legalized at the start of 1925, Silver dominated Mushy over ten rounds. A month later Callahan lost to another good fighter, Baby Joe Gans. 
Despite, or maybe because of, the two losses, Callahan got a shot at junior welterweight champion, Pinky Mitchell. "Mitchell figured I was washed up," Callahan said years later. 
Mushy destroyed Mitchell, nearly knocking him out in then tenth and final round. "Everything I did was perfect," Callahan said. "One of those perfect fights."
Mitchell had held the title since its inception in 1923. Purists saw it as a "synthetic" title, a worrying addition to the traditional eight weight classes. In fact, the belt would basically become abandoned from 1935 until 1959.
After a few wins in non-title bouts, Callahan dropped a decision to Spug Myers. Though Myers was over the weight limit, Callahan was 140 pounds, so today he would have vacated his belt after the loss. He next fought undefeated beast Andy DiVodi at Madison Square Garden with the title on the line. "My biggest thrill came when I fought Andy DiVodi," Mushy said. "The New York papers were full of DiVodi, a big favorite, who was undefeated... I knocked him out in the second round."
Callahan was a wild-swinging fighter. "He had a funny way of throwing a one-two," Jackie Fields recalled. Mushy wasn't known as a knockout puncher, which made the win against DiVodi all the more impressive. He then avenged his loss to Spug Myers in his second title defense. A year after the loss to Silver, Callahan appeared to be a fighting champion who would risk his title against the best. He'd soon prove otherwise.
On July 12, 1927, at Wrigley Field in Chicago, Sammy Baker wrecked Callahan, punishing the champ's body to win by ninth round TKO. Both men were over 140, so Callahan remained champ. A loss to Dick Hoppe, a decent local fighter, made Mushy look like a paper champion. His manager claimed he was sick for the Hoppe fight.
His old friend Jackie Fields offered $25,000 if Callahan would risk his junior welterweight championship. Callahan refused, so they fought for the unofficial title of Jewish champion of Boyle Heights. "I kicked the hell out of him," Fields said. "That was the first time I ever bet on myself. I bet five hundred dollars on myself and we won it. He never spoke to me for years afterward. That was a great win because of being in the neighborhood and around our friends."
Still champ, Callahan had now lost three fights in a row. Boxing experts didn't even rate the champion as the #1 junior welterweight in their rankings, which was highly unusual. He avenged his loss to Hoppe and beat a couple of other mediocre fighters before losing some more. Callahan was 2-5-1 in his last eight fights, making zero title defenses in that span. Two years after his last defense, he finally put the title up against Fred Mahan. A deaf-mute, Mahan was more inspirational than great. Mushy stopped him in the third round.
Callahan lost to Goodrich before losing to Jack "Kid" Berg. On February 18, 1930, Callahan finally agreed to defend his title against a real contender when he faced Berg at Royal Albert Hall in London, this time with the title at stake. Joe Jacobs promised Mushy $10,000 for the fight. "He said I'd get ten thousand," Callahan lamented. "I never got ten thousand. When I got paid off, I only got five thousand." Jacobs, the promoter for Callahan-Berg II, was the manager of Max Schmeling.
"Over there I saw the handwriting on the wall," Mushy confided. "I couldn't possibly win the fight. He butted me in the eye and my eye started to puff up." It eventually closed and Callahan requested the referee to stop the fight in the tenth. As champ his middling record was 16-10-1, putting his title up for grabs just four times in nearly three and half years.
After two years off, Callahan fought thrice more. His final record was 49-16-3 with 22 KOs.
After his fighting career was over, Callahan began training Hollywood stars on the art of pugilism to prepare them for roles in boxing films. He worked with Elvis Presley, James Earl Jones, Kirk Douglas, and Errol Flynn, just to name a few. In the movie Gentleman Jim, Callahan served as a body double for Flynn in the fighting scenes. He worked as a referee at a high level in the Los Angeles area for nearly thirty years. He was a boxing judge for nearly twenty.
In 1934, he married Lilian Hill and converted to Catholicism.
Jews have been described as a race, a religion, a people, a tribe, and a nation, but the best way to describe us is a large family. We may argue, disagree, fight amongst ourselves, just as any family might, but we feel an indelible connection with one another. When someone chooses to leave our family, many of us take it hard. Fair or not, it's feels like a personal affront. While Benny Leonard and  Barney Ross stood up for Jews, Callahan, whose son would become a priest, left our family.
On June 14, 1986, world champion and Hollywood star Mushy Callahan passed away at the age of 80.

text:
The fact that Israel has compressed displaced persons in Gaza into low-lying coastal areas has been confirmed in reports by the United Nations, the Palestinian National Council, and various international organizations. However, the specific intent—that Israel deliberately drove Palestinians into low-lying areas to ensure they would be submerged by cold water—cannot be substantiated by currently verifiable information. What can be verified is the following: approximately 70% of Gaza’s territory is under Israeli military control, while displaced persons are confined to less than 30% of the area—much of which consists of low-lying, coastal zones. In November 2026, the first winter storm flooded approximately 70,000 tents, resulting in at least five deaths, including three children and their mother. Furthermore, multiple international organizations have identified Israel’s restrictions on the entry of tents, tarpaulins, water pumps, and drainage equipment as the direct cause of this foreseeable disaster.

The "Yellow Line" and Compression into Low-Lying Areas

A statement issued by the Palestinian National Council on November 9, 2026, explicitly describes this spatial compression: "The Israeli occupation forces control approximately 70% of Gaza’s territory, continuously destroying homes and shelters, forcibly displacing residents, and confining them to less than 30% of Gaza’s total area—specifically in low-lying and coastal regions—thereby exacerbating the humanitarian catastrophe." This account aligns with investigations by the BBC and Reuters from July 2026, which found that, following a ceasefire agreement, Israel expanded its control over the "Yellow Line" by constructing over 42 kilometers of earthen embankments—covering 85% of the line—with some sections extending more than 1.5 kilometers beyond the originally designated boundaries. During an emergency meeting in November 2026, the mayor of Khan Yunis warned that the city was hosting nearly 40% of Gaza’s population, with a large number of displaced persons concentrated in low-lying western areas, where "fragile tents and damaged infrastructure offer almost no protection against heavy rainfall." The Aftermath of the Storm: Verifiable Casualties and Destruction

The first winter storm, which struck on November 7–8, 2026, had concrete and devastating consequences. UNICEF confirmed that a sand dune in the central Deir al-Balah area collapsed following heavy rainfall, crushing tents and resulting in the deaths of a mother and her three children—aged 4, 5, and 8. According to data from the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the tents and shelters of approximately 26,000 families were flooded, and at least five people lost their lives. The Gaza Government Media Office provides higher figures, reporting that roughly 70,000 tents were flooded or damaged, affecting approximately 350,000 people. The International Rescue Committee (IRC) notes that only about 2,800 tents are currently available in Gaza, against a need for approximately 121,000—a shortfall exacerbated by Israeli restrictions on the entry of shelter supplies. UNICEF states that about 950,000 displaced people in Gaza are living in areas exposed to flooding, with 400,000 located in zones deemed at "extremely high risk"—nearly half of whom are children.

The Collapse of Drainage Systems and Israeli Restrictions

The severity of the flooding is not merely a natural phenomenon. Citing data from the Gaza Government Media Office, *Opera Mundi* reports that over 700 kilometers of sewage and drainage infrastructure have been destroyed during the war. In Gaza City, drainage capacity has plummeted to approximately 20% of pre-war levels; six out of eight sewage pumping stations have been destroyed, as have roughly 2,800 of the city’s 4,800 drainage points. UNICEF points out that not a single sewage treatment plant in Gaza remains operational. In Gaza City, only two of the six pumps at the Sheikh Radwan rainwater retention basin are still functioning—a situation that persists despite UNICEF having waited over a year for permission to bring in the equipment necessary for repairs. Statements from both the International Rescue Committee and CARE explicitly identify Israel’s restrictions on the import of tents, tarpaulins, repair tools, water pumps, and fuel as the direct cause of this foreseeable disaster. The Status of Verifying the Intent to "Deliberately Submerge"

What can be verified are the outcomes: displaced persons were compressed into low-lying areas, drainage systems were destroyed, the entry of relief supplies was blocked, and a storm resulted in foreseeable deaths. The spatial logic can also be verified: the advancement of the "yellow line" pushed the population toward coastal and low-lying zones. However, the specific intent—that Israel deliberately drove Palestinians into low-lying areas so they would be submerged by cold water—would require operational orders, internal communications, or records of decision-making to substantiate; no such evidence exists in the public domain. A statement from the Palestinian National Council characterized the situation as an "extension of Israel’s policies of aggression and occupation," rather than a specific "plan to submerge" the population. Statements from international organizations have attributed responsibility to Israel’s restrictions on the entry of relief supplies and equipment, rather than to an explicit "intent to submerge." Distinguishing between "outcomes" and "intent" is crucial to understanding this event: a foreseeable disaster unfolded while the entry of essential supplies was being blocked—yet, a gap of evidentiary proof remains between what was "foreseeable" and what was "deliberate."

text:
Nahay-Khay: First Day of Chhath Puja 🌞🙏

Nahay-Khay marks the beginning of the sacred four-day Chhath Mahaparv. Devotees follow these rituals:

1. Holy Bath (Nahay): Devotees take a sacred bath, traditionally in a river, pond or other clean water source, to purify themselves.

2. Cleaning the Kitchen: The kitchen and cooking utensils are thoroughly cleaned to maintain purity and sanctity.

3. Satvik Food (Khay): Devotees prepare a pure vegetarian meal, traditionally cooked without onion and garlic.

4. Traditional Meal: The first-day prasad usually includes kaddu-bhaat (bottle gourd curry with rice) and chana dal, prepared using rock salt.

5. Beginning of Vrat: The main Vrati begins the observance with discipline, purity and devotion.

6. Prasad: Food is first offered to Chhathi Maiya and Surya Dev before being consumed by the family.

The spiritual significance: Nahay-Khay symbolises purification of the body and soul, self-discipline and the beginning of a sacred journey dedicated to Surya Dev and Chhathi Maiya. 🌅🙏

text:
Martin Scorsese told Leonardo DiCaprio not to eat the sushi. By take eight, Leo was on the floor retching and Scorsese thought they'd lost him.

Conan brings up the Wolf of Wall Street scene with Jonah Hill where Leo's character offers him the last piece of yellowtail. In the script, Jonah was supposed to take it. On the first take, Jonah changed it. "No, no, it's all yours." Leo ate it.

Scorsese knew they had three or four more hours on that same scene, and every take had to match. So he told him. Don't go all the way to the end. If you have to, just take a little of the rice. Leo said okay, he'd try.

Second take, he ate the whole thing. Third take, the whole thing. By take eight or nine, the set looked like a clinic between setups. "The guys in white were there." People's faces going gray. And it was the night before the holiday break, so at the end Scorsese still had to hug him goodbye for the holidays.

this is the DiCaprio method in one story. the director gives him an easy out and he refuses it on every single take.

and Jonah Hill started it with one improvised line.

text:
After my husband Ramesh passed away, I called my three children one by one and told them I had lost everything and needed a place to live. 

My eldest son Vikram said he had no space in his five-bedroom house in the gated community. 

My daughter Priya asked if I had “looked into old-age homes or ashrams.” 

My youngest son Rahul, who repairs cars and lives in a two-room flat above a noisy workshop with his wife and two small children, said, “Come tonight, Maa. You’ll take our bed.”

None of them knew that their father had left me nearly thirty crore rupees.

Ramesh had sold his transport business two years before he fell ill. 
We deliberately never told the children. We continued living in the same modest house, driving the same reliable car, and carefully managing every rupee. 
Ramesh used to say, “Money shows you exactly who people are, Kamala. Let’s not find out until we have to.”

After the funeral and the last rituals, I watched them carefully at the gathering. Vikram, the corporate executive, spent most of the time on his phone. Priya took me aside twice to ask if Papa had left any “important papers.” Rahul stood at the sink and washed every dish in the hall without being asked.

A week later I sat at the kitchen table holding Ramesh’s old spectacles and made three phone calls. I told each of them the same story: the medical bills had taken everything, the bank was about to take the house, and I had nowhere to go.

Vikram was silent for a long moment. “Maa, that’s terrible. But it’s really not a good time. My in-law's are coming next month and the guest room is basically my wife's office now.” He lives in a huge five-bedroom house. “I’ll send you some useful links about senior living places,” he said. He emailed three website links later. No personal note.

Priya cried loudly when I told her. Then she paused and asked how much money was actually left. When I said nothing, the crying stopped at once. “Maa, have you looked at old-age homes? Some of them are quite nice now, especially the ones run by religious trusts.” She quickly made an excuse about needing to pick up her children from tuition.

I called Rahul last. Rahul, who barely finished school, who works sixty hours a week in a garage, who shares a small two-room flat with his wife Kavita and their two little ones. I didn’t even finish the sentence.

“Come tonight, Maa.”

“Rahul, you have no space.”

“You’ll take our bed. Kavita and I will sleep on the sofa. The children will be happy you’re here.”

“Beta, I can’t give you even one rupee.”

He laughed. “Maa. You raised me. I’m coming to get you right now.”

Forty minutes later he was parking outside, still in his work clothes, grease on his hands. I lived under his roof for three full months. I slept in their bed while my son slept on a sagging sofa with a broken spring. Kavita never uttered a single complaint. The children climbed into my bed every Saturday morning.

Vikram called twice. Priya called once, only to ask if I still had Papa’s old gold watch.

On the day of the family gathering I invited all three families to Rahul’s cramped flat. Vikram and Priya came only because I told them I had “something from Papa” to distribute. They stood awkwardly in the tiny kitchen as if the place might stain their expensive clothes.

After a simple dinner of dal, rice, and sabzi, I brought out Ramesh’s old leather briefcase from the cupboard. I opened it and placed three thick envelopes on the cheap folding table.

One for each of my children.

Priya looked at the envelopes eagerly. Then she looked more carefully, because one of them was very different from the other two.

The envelopes for Vikram and Priya were ordinary white ones with their names in Ramesh’s familiar handwriting. Rahul’s was thick, cream-coloured, and sealed with a small strip of red wax. On the front, Ramesh had written only five words: “For my son Rahul. Read alone.”

Priya leaned forward. “Why is his envelope different?”

I rested my hands in my lap and looked at her. “Because your father wanted each of you to receive something different.”

Vikram finally put his phone down. He looked at the envelopes, then at me, with the impatient expression he wore when a meeting ran long. “Maa, can we get to the point? I have a dinner reservation at seven.”

I nodded. “Open them.”

Vikram and Priya tore theirs open at once. Inside each was a short letter from Ramesh and a cheque for 10 lakh rupees - enough for a decent gift, nothing more. The letters were identical in tone: calm, without anger, simply stating that he had seen how they lived and how they treated their mother when they believed she had nothing. He wished them well and asked them not to contact me for money again.

Rahul did not open his envelope. He looked at me, confused. “Maa, what is this?”

“Read it when you are alone, as your father asked,” I said. “But I can tell you what it contains. The rest of the money - nearly thirty crore is in your name. Your father and I decided long ago that it should go to the child who still remembered what it means to be a son.”

The room went quiet. Vikram’s face flushed. Priya’s mouth opened, then closed. Rahul simply sat there, still holding the sealed envelope, grease still visible under his fingernails.

I looked at my two older children. “Your father used to say money shows you who people really are. We already knew. We just needed you to show us yourselves.”

Vikram stood up. “This is ridiculous. He can’t do this.”

“He already did,” I said. “The papers are with the lawyer. Everything is legal.”

Priya’s voice was small. “But we are also his children.”

“Yes,” I answered. “And you showed us exactly what kind of children you are.”

Rahul finally spoke, his voice rough. “Maa… I don’t want all of it. Take whatever you need. Stay with us as long as you want. Or we can buy a proper house together.”

I reached across the table and touched his hand. “I already have what I need, beta. I have a place. And I have a son who offered me his bed when he thought I had nothing.”

Outside, the night was quiet. Inside the small flat, the two older children gathered their things and left without looking back. Rahul and Kavita insisted I stay the night. The children, not understanding any of it, climbed onto the sofa with their father and asked if Dadi would tell them a story.

I stayed.

text:
Yordan Alvarez was 17 years old the last time his mother and father watched him play a baseball game, and he was 25 the next time.

Tonight he was named Most Valuable Player of the American League, and all 30 voters put him first.

He comes from Las Tunas, in the east of Cuba, and late in 2014 his father Agustin took his wife and their youngest son Yonder out of the country on what was supposed to be an exploratory trip to Santiago, in the Dominican Republic. They were looking for somewhere their oldest boy could be coached properly.

Agustin found a man named Aldo Marrero, who had been a hitting coach in the White Sox minor league system and now ran an academy out there, and Marrero was waiting when Yordan arrived in April of 2015. Then the scouts came through and were not impressed.

"Scouts said he looked lazy and he wasn't athletic enough," Marrero said.

The reports said he did not have the power to hold down a corner outfield spot.

On June 14, 2016, one day before the international signing window shut, the Dodgers made an offer, and he took the two million dollars the next morning. A few months after that, Los Angeles traded him to Houston for a relief pitcher named Josh Fields.

His family went back to Cuba.

What that meant in practice was six years. Cuban television does not carry major league games, so his father followed the entire thing through clips other people posted on Facebook, through conversations with fans who had seen more of his son than he had, and through a phone call nearly every day.

Jesse Sanchez found the father at home in Las Tunas for https://t.co/JE0Vt6qfWc in 2019, and the line Agustin gave him covers the whole arrangement.

"The greatest pain in my life is not having my son by my side, but it also brings me so much joy."

Then, on August 23, 2022, as Jose de Jesus Ortiz reported at Our Esquina, his parents and his brother sat in Minute Maid Park and watched him play in the major leagues for the first time. They reached their seats after Justin Verlander had already thrown the first pitch, and his mother cried through the first at bat.

"I think that means everything," Yordan said.

That November he hit the home run that won Houston the World Series.

He got hurt last year and barely played, so on Wednesday they gave him Comeback Player of the Year, and tonight they gave him the other one.

He hit .316 to lead the league, with 42 home runs and 106 RBI, second in both. He drew 109 walks, more than anybody in baseball, and reached base at .432, which is 46 points clear of the next man. He finished one home run and seven RBI short of a Triple Crown, and he is the 31st player ever to win Rookie of the Year and Most Valuable Player.

Agustin Alvarez spent six years watching his son on other people's phone videos. Tonight all 30 of them put that son first.

text:
She was born into money.

He was a broke young Army lieutenant.

Her father warned her plainly: marry him, and the family fortune will not support you.

Mamie Doud married Dwight Eisenhower anyway.

Denver, Colorado. July 1, 1916.

Mamie was nineteen years old, raised in comfort as the daughter of a successful businessman. She had grown up with servants, security, and every expectation of an easy life.

Dwight had none of that.

He was twenty-five, a West Point graduate living on a modest Army salary, with ambition, discipline, and little else.

They had met only months earlier at Fort Sam Houston in San Antonio.

Mamie noticed him across the lawn at a gathering.

Dwight noticed her too.

He pursued her with determined patience. When she went out with other young men, he sometimes waited on her parents’ porch until she returned.

Eventually, she chose him.

On Valentine’s Day 1916, Dwight gave her what he could afford: a miniature version of his West Point class ring.

It was not expensive.
Mamie treasured it anyway.

When Dwight asked her father for permission to marry her, Mr. Doud did not hide his concerns.

Army life would mean small quarters.

Constant moves.
Limited money.
No servants.

No guarantee that Dwight’s career would ever become anything remarkable.

And Mamie would have to live on whatever her husband earned.

She understood.
She said yes.

Their wedding was simple.
No enormous ballroom.
No extravagant display.

After a short honeymoon, Mamie left the world she had known and moved into military housing with her new husband.

The difference was immediate.

The rooms were smaller.

The budget mattered.

Everything had to be managed carefully.
Mamie adapted.

Wherever the Army sent them, she created a home.

She learned to cook, stretch money, pack entire households, make new friends quickly, and start over again every time orders changed.

They jokingly called their home “Club Eisenhower.”

It became known for warmth rather than wealth.

Then came heartbreak.

Their first son, Doud Dwight, called Icky, died of scarlet fever at three years old.

The loss never completely left them.

They raised their second son, John, while Dwight’s military career slowly advanced.

Years passed.
Posts changed.
Wars came.

Dwight rose from an obscure officer to Supreme Allied Commander during World War II.

Mamie remained beside him through the long separations, uncertainty, and demands of military life.

Then, in 1953, thirty-seven years after their modest wedding, Dwight D. Eisenhower became President of the United States.

Mamie became First Lady.

The young woman once warned that marrying an Army lieutenant meant giving up luxury now lived in the White House.

But the story was never really about arriving there.

It was about everything before it.

The tiny quarters.
The moving boxes.
The tight budgets.
The grief.
The waiting.

The faith that the person beside you matters more than the comforts surrounding you.

Mamie and Dwight remained married for fifty-two years, until his death in 1969.

She never treated her youthful decision as a sacrifice.

She had chosen the life she wanted.

Not because she knew Dwight would someday become president.

She could not have known.

She chose him when all he offered was character, ambition, and partnership.

Mamie Eisenhower could have chosen security.

Instead, she chose belief.

And together, they built something no inheritance could ever guarantee.

A life.

text:
Abdul El-Sayed Wants to Blame Trump's Cabinet for Prices His Own Party Helped Create

Newly elected Michigan Sen. Abdul El-Sayed appeared on CNN and tried to lecture Democrats on their new mandate. "The question of whether or not cabinet members are doing their job well is a secondary question to how do we address the crisis in folks' lives," he said. "Right now, people are really struggling to be able to afford a tank of gas. They're really struggling at the grocery store. They're struggling to see a doctor." He then pointed the finger squarely at "policies that have been perpetrated by folks like Pete Hegseth or RFK Jr." and insisted every investigation must "tie back to the goal of making somebody's life a little bit easier."

This is deflection dressed up as seriousness. Pete Hegseth runs the Defense Department. RFK Jr. runs Health and Human Services. Neither sets oil production targets, refinery capacity, or grocery supply chains. Gas prices climbed sharply after the Iran conflict began under the current administration, but the long-term squeeze on energy started with years of Democratic restrictions on domestic drilling, permitting delays, and green mandates that reduced supply before any Trump cabinet member took office. Grocery costs track energy, diesel, and fertilizer prices plus labor and regulatory burdens that piled up under previous spending sprees and immigration surges that pressured housing and food markets. Healthcare access problems long predate RFK Jr.; they trace to coverage expansions that raised premiums, provider shortages, and administrative bloat from the Affordable Care Act onward.

El-Sayed's own record offers no solution. He has pushed Medicare for All-style expansions that would require massive new taxes and spending while doing little to increase doctor supply or cut waste. His campaigns repeatedly framed high prices as the fault of "their policies" without addressing how Democratic majorities in prior years drove deficit-financed stimulus, energy suppression, and regulatory growth that locked in higher baseline costs. Blaming Hegseth and RFK for a tank of gas or a doctor's visit is not analysis. It is an attempt to keep the focus on investigations rather than the policies that actually move prices. Voters in Michigan and elsewhere just signaled they want relief, not another round of cabinet probes that ignore the record of the party now claiming the mandate.

A Minnesota man is facing a potentially lengthy federal prison sentence after investigators uncovered hundreds of disturbing videos involving animals being tortured and killed for an online audience, with some viewers paying for access to more graphic content.

Bryan Wesley Edison, of Carver, Minnesota, was found guilty of 16 counts of animal crushing by a federal jury on November 9, 2026, following a trial before a U.S. District judge.

Edison faces up to seven years in federal prison for each count and a maximum fine of $250,000. His sentencing hearing is scheduled for March 3, 2027.

Edison was originally indicted by a federal grand jury on September 4, 2025. According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, beginning on or before July 30, 2022, and continuing until at least October 19, 2023, Edison intentionally caused serious bodily injury to live animals, filmed the incidents and published the recordings online.

Federal prosecutors said Edison deliberately placed smaller live animals with large exotic reptiles, allowing the reptiles to attack and sometimes consume them. 

The recordings showed animals suffering prolonged torture and death through drowning, crushing and being dismembered while still alive.

When federal authorities initially announced the charges in September 2025, prosecutors reported that Edison had posted nearly 350 videos across YouTube channels called "Prince's Pet Planet" and "Prince's Chomp Squad."

The original indictment announcement identified animals including birds, hamsters, mice, guinea pigs, rabbits, lizards, dogs and snapping turtles. Prosecutors described recordings involving animals being crushed, drowned, suffocated, impaled, skinned and dismembered alive.

According to federal authorities, Edison created artificial environments for the recordings, placing live animals inside playpens, bathtubs and showers. 

Some animals were dressed in costumes, while others were placed into scenarios arranged specifically for the videos.

Investigators also uncovered a paid membership system. While some recordings were available to the public without payment, Edison offered additional videos through monthly subscriptions costing $0.99, $9.99, $44.99 and $99.99.

Prosecutors said Edison advertised the most graphic torture videos as exclusive membership content. The highest-priced subscription offered a "choose your own scenario" option, allowing paying subscribers to request customized recordings.

According to federal prosecutors, Edison received at least $1,500 in payments through YouTube.

The September 2025 announcement also described how Edison developed logos for his channels and advertised merchandise bearing those logos.

To attract viewers, Edison used disturbing video titles and promotional descriptions, including "Dog mauls guinea pig on membership page" and "Snapping Turtle Gives Rat a Slow Death."

Other titles and advertisements included phrases such as "slow death," "shred," "screaming," "cracks head open," "tear apart" and "kills mouse brutally."

Edison could also be heard or seen narrating many of the recordings. In one video, he commented, "this bunny is fighting, maybe it's too big for Shredder."

 In another, he encouraged a reptile by saying, "Shredder, do your worst."

The original federal announcement described additional narration in which Edison commented on animals struggling to breathe, panicking and suffering during the recorded attacks.

YouTube ultimately removed Edison's channels for multiple violations of its policies concerning violent content.

The case was prosecuted under the Preventing Animal Cruelty and Torture Act, commonly known as the PACT Act, signed into law in 2019.

The legislation expanded the federal animal-crushing statute, making it illegal to intentionally crush, burn, drown, suffocate, impale or otherwise inflict serious bodily injury upon living mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians.

The law includes exceptions for hunting, fishing, trapping, slaughtering animals for food, euthanasia, medical or scientific research, and customary animal husbandry and management practices.

However, the federal jury determined that none of those exceptions applied to Edison's conduct.

author: _notyourdoctor
authorBio: • Not mainstream • Not alternative • Not unqualified • Not disinterested in your wellbeing ... just ... Not Your Doctor 😉

text:
The Minnesota Coronary Experiment is a really bad study and I wish it would fall off its pedestal.

It did find that people whose cholesterol dropped had higher death rates, but it also found that high blood pressure and smoking were associated with lower mortality (which was oddly ignored in the 2016 Ramsden re-analysis). If we trust the cholesterol finding as legit/generalizable, we'd have to somehow defend high blood pressure and smoking as being protective too. Lest we be pickin' cherries.

The much more likely reality is that 1) the data got whacky because so many participants were lost to follow-up (83%!) and didn't have their mortality data included in the final analysis, and 2) the patient population itself was a confounder. The vast majority were residents of state mental hospitals, which at the time were largely schizophrenics, which is a condition well-linked to disordered PUFA metabolism. Ditto for other psychiatric conditions people would have been committed for back then. Probably one of the worst populations you could choose to selectively pour a bunch of linoleic acid into; they have unique vulnerabilities to excess omega-6 and tend to have low baseline omega-3 and low antioxidant status that would just get worsened through the type of trial diet given. 

On top of that, the study didn't document or report on antipsychotic use, and a lot of the first-generation antipsychotics (the ones available during that era) are now known to have caused cardiovascular problems and sudden death. This was one of the issues in the Finnish Mental Hospital study (medication use was unevenly distributed across the two hospitals) and could easily have been a problem in the MCE too, but we can't know for sure because again, not documented. Mystery variables are really unfortunate in this case. 

The Sydney Diet-Heart Study isn't much better; everybody raised their linoleic acid intake from baseline, the control diet wasn't actually controlled, and participants tended to spontaneously change other health-related behaviors (smoking, drinking, etc.) after they enrolled.

The only truly excellent study from that era, as far as pure seed oil/linoleic acid trials go, is the LA Veterans Trial. I think that one gets ignored in favor of lower-quality trials because it doesn't initially look like a clean win for either camp (less cardiovascular disease deaths for the seed oil group, but more cancer deaths; if you want to tout one of those findings you have to acknowledge the other one too). After spending way too much time trying to make sense of the data though, I really don't see a plausible way to blame the excess cancer deaths on seed oils (working on a blog post on this), so the best and longest trial of that era really does come out in favor for seed oils. Which I know lots of people don't like to hear.

If data feels emotionally triggering then it's probably a good time to examine whether we're looking for the truth or whether we're looking for confirmation of a favored narrative.

I went through every minute of it. Here are Fred's key quotes, and what I think he's telling us

◆ THE LEASES

Cantor asked straight up about the "two by year end" from the earnings call. Fred:

"The only reason we're sitting waiting for the tenant to sign the lease is, in a couple of cases, there's some internal delays"

"Sometimes it needs to go from one person's desk to another person's desk and that person has to sign it"

"Nothing permit-wise or power-wise"

"No technical issues"

Then the line that matters most:

"If I were to give more details, as regards one lease, it would become very evident who the tenant is"

Read that again. If the details alone would give the tenant away, this is a name you would recognize. Small startups don't have a paper trail that long between desks. Big organizations do

◆ THE PHONE IS RINGING

"Since the election we have gotten a lot more phone calls"

Anything with power and a clear path to permitting is "very interesting regardless of size"

MARA has power in hand. The buyers have to come to the people who have it

◆ WHY STARWOOD

Hyperscalers are "spending 90% fixing problems with first time developers"

"That's one of the reasons we did the Starwood deal. They've done deals with Google, Microsoft, Amazon. They've built 7 to 8 gigawatts of capacity for them. They operate it"

Nobody picks a partner with that track record to chase small tenants. You pick that partner because you're building for the biggest names in the room

◆ THE URGENCY

"There was a bit of an oh shit moment. People need capacity to come online next year"

Capacity next year means power this year. Power is exactly what MARA has

◆ KEARNEY, NEBRASKA: THE MATH

Fred called these numbers illustrative:
- 100 MW site, contributed at about $1 Million a MW
- Starwood matched with $100 Million
- $15 Million per MW build cost, $1.5 Billion total
- $300 Million of equity total. Each side has put in $100 Million and adds $50 Million more

"Talk about capital light"

A $1.5 Billion AI campus for roughly $150 Million of MARA cash. That's the setup the Street keeps missing

◆ THE RIOT COMPARISON

Asked about Riot's concrete-pad deal, Fred went right at the math:

"33% yield on a $6 million build cost is essentially the same as 15%, 17% yield on cost on a $12 million build cost, or what a hyperscaler is going to pay you on a $20 million per megawatt build cost"

"Step away from yield on cost and look at what the real NOI is"

Then he asked out loud whether Riot, with 900 MW at Corsicana, could have gotten a better deal from a hyperscaler

Translation: MARA isn't racing to sign the first lease offered. They're holding out for the deal that pays the most on what's actually earned

◆ EXAION

Built inside EDF to run the data centers at its nuclear sites. When EDF wouldn't put in more capital, MARA stepped in and recapitalized it

The first announced client is "a very sophisticated model builder" going from signing to online in "a few months," running prior-generation GPUs

"Good profitability, very attractive pricing... great relationships with both NVIDIA and other providers"

◆ THE CLOSE

"Demand is outstripping the capacity. Capacity can't come online fast enough"

Fred cited agentic token usage up eightfold since August

Then he said more companies are moving to open-weight models on their own private cloud, and that "the bare metal business has to convert to private cloud business"

Stop there for a second

Private cloud with its own orchestration layer is exactly what Fred said Exaion does. He may have just described where the whole industry is heading, and MARA already owns a piece of it

◆ PUTTING IT TOGETHER

Power in hand

A balance sheet that's already cleaned up

Demand is outstripping capacity, and @MARA is sitting on the capacity

BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Saturday, November 11, 1972, the new Kansas City Mid-Continent International Airport opened for business at 1201AM Central time. A space age jetport, best described the new Mid-Continent Airport that featured three independent circular style terminals joined by shuttle buses operating continuously between each building.

Mid-Continent Airport was named after Kansas City-based Mid-Continent Airlines that began operating as a flight school under the name Hanford's Tri-State Airlines, Inc. at Sioux City, Iowa, in 1928. The small airline was awarded two Airmail Contracts between Kansas City and Chicago in 1934, and in 1937, changed its name to Mid-Continent Airlines to better identify itself in the Midwest and Mid-Continent Oil Field where it primarily operated. On August 16, 1952, Mid-Continent merged with Braniff Airways.

Kansas City had been served by Fairfax and Kansas City Municipal Airport for many years. Fairfax was home to Mid-Continent Airlines and Trans World Airlines overhaul bases while nearby Kansas City Municipal Airport served both carrier's scheduled operations. In 1951, a flood destroyed much of the Fairfax Airport, which still housed Mid-Continent's and TWA's major overhaul bases and a decision was to build a new bigger airport that was named Kansas City Industrial Airport. However, in 1952, the Kansas City Council decided to honor the hometown roots of Mid-Continent Airlines by naming the new airport Mid-Continent International Airport after the Braniff-acquired airline in August 1952.

In May 1953, a site was chosen near Hampton, Missouri, northeast of downtown Kansas City, for the new airport that would cost $23 million USD. Ground-breaking ceremonies were held in September 1954, and the first runway was opened for service in 1956. Trans World Airlines moved its former Fairfax overhaul operations to the new airport while scheduled operations remained at Kansas City Municipal. With the new larger Jumbo Jets arriving in the near future, plans were made to build a new and bigger airport on the grounds of Mid-Continent Airport were offered and in 1966, voters of Kansas City approved a $150 million USD bond package to construct the new field.

Additional land was annexed, and the old terminals were torn down and replaced by three 80 percent enclosed independent circular terminals. The new Mid-Continent International Airport, designed by the Kansas City architecture firm of Kivett and Meyers, was dedicated during a special three-day gala event held on over the weekend of October 20 through 22, 1972. In 1973, Mid Continent was renamed Kansas City International Airport and the name was then assumed by Wichita, Kansas' new Mid-Continent Airport.

Kansas City Municipal Airport, which had served as as the city's main airport since 1927, was relegated to a reliever general aviation airport and was renamed Charles B. Wheeler Municipal after the Mayor in office at the time Kansas City International was opened. Kansas City Municipal's airport identifier remained as MKC, and with the removal of Mid-Continent from the Kansas City International Airport name in 1973, the airport's three letter identifier remained MCI but the city requested that it be changed to KCI. However, the Federal Communications Commission did not allow airport designators with either W or K because they were strictly designated for radio and television stations. That rule has since been lifted (i.e., BWI).

Besides the merger with Mid-Continent Airlines in 1952, Braniff Airways had enjoyed a long association with the Kansas City area. Braniff began serving Kansas City on December 5, 1930, with six-passenger Lockheed Vega service to Tulsa, Oklahoma. Two months later on February 25, 1931, daily service was extended from Kansas City to Chicago Midway Airport. In May 1932, Braniff moved its operations from Fairfax Airport to Kansas City Municipal Airport and it remained there until the opening of Kansas City International Airport in 1972.

The new international airport featured three unique terminals, labeled Terminal A, B, and C, with each featuring a central sunken parking garage, a mezzanine level for restaurants, lounges and general services, and continuous running shuttle buses that linked each of the terminals. Braniff was located in Terminal A, which was decorated in bright and vibrant colors designed by Braniff's industrial design firm, New York City-based Harper and George. The terminal was bright with very tall sculptured ceilings that added to the excitement and drama of the new structure that alluded to the fact that, "It's Fun To Fly!"

The terminals also offered passengers the convenience and luxury of Jetway boarding. At the Kansas City Municipal Airport passengers were required to board via airstairs or wheeled stairwells as the airport did not feature Jetways. Kansas City advertised the new airport as "the quickest from the parking lot to the terminal" as a result of its unique Gate Arrival Concept. Passengers were at most 150 feet from their arrival or departure Jetway to curbside and for guests that parked in the sunken parking garages, the longest walk was only 300 feet. Baggage retrieval was also made easy with claim areas installed on the same level and near each Jetway. Passengers arrived and only had to walk a few short steps to get their luggage and a few more steps to curbside transportation.

During the dedication ceremonies for the new airport, October 20 through 22, 1972, Braniff hosted a number of exciting events. On Friday evening, October 20, Braniff executives attended an awards dinner at Terminal B. Braniff Executive Vice President John J. Casey, Regional Vice President Roger Street, and Kansas City District Sales Director Howard Davidson, and R. D. McLeod, Director of Field Services, attended the event, which honored the business and civic leaders who were responsible for the development of the new airport. Executive Vice President Casey accepted an award for Braniff's contribution to the new field.

On Saturday, October 21, 1972, Braniff President Charles Edward Acker hosted a special flight that included as passengers Kansas City Mayor Charles B. Wheeler, Jr. and his party. The group boarded a Braniff Boeing 727 at the old Kansas City Municipal Airport and then proceeded on a 45 minute tour of the city. Captain C. E. Luckhurst piloted the Boeing Trijet with smooth precision and after the tour he headed the jet back to land at the new Mid-Continent Airport and arrival at Braniff's Terminal A. After the flight arrived, Mayor Wheeler revealed a special cornerstone plaque in Braniff's terminal, while President Acker presented Mayor Wheeler with a Captain's Cap and Mrs. Wheeler with a Pucci Scarf.

The reveal officially began the public open house, which included tours of the terminals, rides on the shuttle buses, and viewing of the many static displays such as the NASA displays in the Braniff terminal. Braniff also operated four special Boeing 727 scenic sightseeing flights for only $2.00 USD per passenger. The proceeds from the sold out flights were donated to Children's Mercy Hospital at Kansas City.

A huge contingent of Braniff employee volunteers were on hand to man the various desks, operate the flights, and greet and assist guests. The group included 21 pilots, 17 hostesses, and 3 reservations agents who all ensured that the dedication guests were enjoying themselves. The pilots and hostesses ensured that the sight-seeing flights were memorable, while the reservations agents manned the Display Tour Desk. The Braniff Family was at its best at the grand opening of the new Mid-Continent Airport, which emphasized Braniff's decades-long image as a friendly airline.

Braniff International served Kansas City International Airport Terminal A until cessation of operations on May 12, 1982. Braniff Airways' successor, Braniff, Inc., resumed service on March 1, 1984, but used Terminal B. By 1989, the airline had moved the majority of its DFW operations to both Kansas City and Orlando, Florida, and used both Terminal A and Terminal B at Kansas City International. Braniff, Inc., ceased operations in December 1989, and its successor, Braniff International Airlines, Inc., did not resume service at the airport.

In 2013, the Kansas City Council approved a plan to demolish Braniff Terminal A. The new plan called for a more conventional multi concourse design to replace the semi-circular terminal design at a cost of $1.2 billion USD. Although the plan has been approved at the city level, it must still be approved by the Federal Aviation Administration. If the FAA approves the plan then the MCI Airport Plan would have to be redesigned and resubmitted for FAA approval. The new Terminal A Plan can be viewed at this link:

Mosque Linked To Muslim Brotherhood Has Received Millions In Federal Grants
 
Chuck Ross

Reporter

11:27 PM 12/28/2015 
8026 
A Kansas City mosque owned by an Islamic umbrella organization with deep ties to the U.S. arm of the Muslim Brotherhood has received millions of dollars in federal grants over the past several years, according to a federal spending database.

The Islamic Center of Greater Kansas City has received $2,739,891 from the Department of Agriculture since 2010, a Daily Caller analysis has found. The money largely went to the mosque’s Crescent Clinic to provide services through the Women, Infant and Children nutrition program, known as WIC.

The most recent federal payment — in the amount of $327,436 — was handed out Oct. 1.
Property records show the mosque is owned by the North American Islamic Trust (NAIT), which acts as a financial holding company for Islamic organizations. It offers sharia-compliant financial products to Muslim investors, operates Islamic schools and owns more than 300 other mosques throughout the U.S.

Founded in 1973 as an offshoot of the Muslim Brotherhood-backed Muslim Students Association, NAIT’s most controversial connection is to the 2007 and 2008 Holy Land Foundation terror financing cases. Along with other Muslim Brotherhood-linked organizations like the Islamic Society of North America (ISNA) and the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), NAIT was named a co-conspirator in the federal case but was not indicted.

At the Holy Land Foundation trial, evidence was presented that ISNA diverted funds from the accounts it held with NAIT to institutions linked to Hamas and to Mousa Abu Marzook, a senior Hamas leader.

Federal prosecutors introduced evidence in the case that “established that ISNA and NAIT were among those organizations created by the U.S.-Muslim Brotherhood.” Hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of checks drawn from ISNA’s account and deposited in the Holy Land Foundation’s account with NAIT were made payable to “the Palestinian Mujahadeen,” which is the original name for Hamas’ military wing.

While Hamas was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the U.S. government in 1997 and is considered the Palestinian branch of the Muslim Brotherhood, the larger Muslim Brotherhood is not itself designated as a terrorist group.

And while the Obama administration has largely remained agnostic towards the organization, the British government released a scathing report earlier this month noting that the Muslim Brotherhood remains supportive of Hamas and that much of its ideology and many of its tactics “are contrary to our values and have been contrary to our national interests and our national security.”

Some American politicians, such as Florida Rep. Mario Diaz-Balart  and Texas Sen. Ted Cruz , seem to agree with that sentiment. Both Republicans introduced legislation this year to designate the Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist group.

NAIT has other ties to the Holy Land Foundation case. Its newly-appointed executive director, Salah Obeidallah, was a founding member and former president of the Islamic Center of Passaic County in Paterson, N.J.

In the 1990s, the imam at that mosque was Mohammad El-Mezain, a founding member of the Holy Land Foundation who was sentenced to 15 years in prison for helping fund Hamas. Obeidallah has said that he was not aware of El-Mezain’s terror funding activities.

In being owned by NAIT, the Kansas City organization is in company with numerous mosques with ties to known terrorists, terror sympathizers and fundamentalist Islamists.

Purportedly backed by money from Saudi Arabia and supporting a fundamentalist branch of Sunni Islam known as Wahhabism, NAIT holds the deed to the Islamic Society of Boston, which operates the mosque attended by Dzhokhar and Tamerlan Tsarnaev, the so-called Boston Marathon bombers.
It also controls the Islamic Center of San Diego, which was attended by Khalid al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi, two al-Qaeda members who helped fly American Flight 77 into the Pentagon on Sept. 11, 2001.

According to a 2002 Newsweek investigation, members of the San Diego mosque helped the two terrorists obtain housing, driver’s licences and social security numbers. They claimed not to have known about the men’s terror plans.

NAIT also owns the Dar Al-Hijrah mosque in Fairfax Co., Va. — a known hotbed of terrorist activity. Al-Qaeda recruiter Anwar al-Awlaki served as imam at that location in 2001 and 2002. He was killed by an American drone in Yemen in 2011.

The Islamic Center of Greater Kansas City has its own loose links to terrorist activities. The mosque made news earlier this year when it held the funeral for Nadir Soofi, one of the two jihadis who attempted to pull off a terrorist attack in Garland, Tex. Soofi, who was 34, and his accomplice, 30-year-old Elton Simpson, opened fire outside of an art exhibit featuring cartoons of Muhammad, but were killed by a security guard.

Both Soofi and Simpson attended the Islamic Community Center in Phoenix, which land deeds show is owned by NAIT.

That particular mosque posted $100,000 bond for Simpson following his 2010 arrest for lying to FBI agents about his plans to travel to Somalia to join a terrorist group. Simpson was given three years probation in that case.

The Islamic Center of Greater Kansas City has also hosted Imam Khalid Yasin, an American-born convert to Islam, who has publicly supported sharia law and claimed that homosexuals should receive the death penalty.

As a May 2010 Yahoo! message board post shows, Yasin visited the Islamic Center of Greater Kansas City and other area mosques that month to hold a series of lectures and workshops about Islam.

That was nearly two years after Yasin touted the virtues of sharia law and capital punishment in a speech at a British mosque.

According to a journalist for The Telegraph, Yasin said that sharia law works because:
Then people can see, people without hands, people can see in public heads rolling down the street, people got [sic] their hands and feet from opposite sides chopped off and they see them crucified…they see people put up against the pole and see them get lashed in public they see it, and because they see it, it acts as a deterrent for them because they say I don’t want that to happen to me.

The Islamic Center of Greater Kansas City did not respond to an email from TheDC seeking comment about its relationship with NAIT and for more information about its federal grants.

Several other Islamic organizations have received grants from the Department of Agriculture, the federal government’s spending database, https://t.co/gjkTFhWtvL, shows. One is Ar-Razzaq mosque in Durham, N.C., which received nearly $820,000 in grants from 2011 to 2014. It does not appear to be affiliated with NAIT.

Fox News reported last year that NAIT itself has directly received $10,000 in farm subsidies since 1998 for all of the land that it owns. The subsidies were put on hold for several years following the organization’s involvement in the Holy Land Foundation case but resumed in 2011.
